orig_9709_s1_count_distinct_arrangements.description: Count arrangements of distinct objects with factorials or choices by position. Split restrictions into cases and use the matching probability denominator.

sections.title: When should I multiply, and when should I add?
sections.label: Count by slots and cases
sections.intro:
First define one complete outcome. For a row, code or set of different roles, changing the order usually changes the outcome. Label the positions so each finished arrangement is counted exactly once.

If there are \(a\) choices for the first step and exactly \(b\) permitted continuations after each first choice, the count is \(ab\). The actual available objects may change; the number of continuations must be the stated one. If that number differs between first choices, split into cases.

blocks.html: Multiply the steps within one case; add disjoint cases. Each complete outcome must appear once. The word “or” alone does not justify adding overlapping counts, and this counting rule does not require probabilistic independence.

blocks.title: Add cases with different continuation counts
blocks.prompt: A code contains one letter followed by one digit. If the letter is X or Y, the digit may be \(1,2\) or \(3\). If the letter is Z, the digit may be \(2\) or \(4\). How many codes are possible?
blocks.hint: Separate the \(\frac{X}{Y}\) case from the Z case. Each finished code belongs to exactly one of these cases.
blocks.solution:
1. Starting with X or Y gives \(2\cdot3=6\) codes. Starting with Z gives \(1\cdot2=2\) codes.

  2. \[6+2=8.\]

    There are not three digit choices after every letter, so one product of \(3\cdot3\) would be invalid.

sections.title: When do I use a factorial or a partial permutation?
sections.label: Factorials and ordered choices
sections.intro:
For a nonnegative integer \(n\), the number of arrangements of \(n\) distinct objects in a full linear row is \(n!\). For \(n\ge1\),

\[n!=n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots2\cdot1.\]

Also \(0!=1\): there is one way to leave zero positions empty. Swapping distinct objects creates a different arrangement; reversing a row does not identify it with the original row.

To fill only \(r\) labelled positions from \(n\) distinct objects without reuse, stop after \(r\) choices:

\[{}^{n}\mathrm{P}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}=n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1),\qquad0\le r\le n.\]

Here \(n,r\) are integers; when \(r=0\), the product is empty and equals one. If \(r>n\), the requested arrangement is impossible, with count zero; do not substitute into a negative factorial.

blocks.html:
If one specified object must appear among the \(r\) positions, choose its position first, then fill the others:

\[r\cdot{}^{n-1}\mathrm{P}_{r-1},\qquad1\le r\le n.\]

This assumes its position is otherwise unrestricted and all objects are distinct. With zero positions, requiring an object makes the count zero.

If reuse is allowed and each of \(r\) positions can contain any of \(n\ge1\) symbols, there are \(n^r\) strings. State the repetition rule first. Distinct labelled roles also have an order: choosing a chair and a secretary is different from selecting an unordered pair.

blocks.title: Count only the positions actually filled
blocks.prompt: Six distinct badges are available, including a badge labelled A. Count four-position displays without reuse, first without any further restriction and then requiring badge A. Also state how many arrangements fill zero positions and how many fill seven positions without reuse.
blocks.hint: For four positions, stop the descending product after four factors. If A is required, choose its position first. Empty placement is one arrangement; seven distinct badges cannot be chosen from only six.
blocks.solution:
1. \[{}^{6}\mathrm{P}_{4}=\frac{6!}{2!}=6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=360.\]

  2. Place A in one of four positions, then fill the others from the five remaining badges:

    \[4\cdot{}^{5}\mathrm{P}_{3}=4\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=240.\]

  3. There is one empty arrangement, so \({}^{6}\mathrm{P}_{0}=1\).

  4. Filling seven positions without reuse is impossible: the count is zero. Do not try to evaluate a factorial of a negative integer.

sections.title: How do I handle positions, separation and relative order?
sections.label: Position restrictions
sections.intro:
Place named objects with fixed positions first. If \(k\) different objects occupy \(k\) distinct prescribed positions and no other restrictions remain, arrange the other \(n-k\) objects in \((n-k)!\) ways. Conflicting instructions, such as two different objects both occupying one position, give zero arrangements.

For forbidden positions, count permitted cases directly or subtract forbidden arrangements from the unrestricted total. If two forbidden cases overlap, subtracting both removes the overlap twice; restore it once. Check whether a named object has a specific end or may occupy either end.

blocks.html:
Place five distinct cards \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), \(D\), \(E\) in a row. Require \(A\) not first and \(B\) not last.

Forbidden positions

Excluded caseCompletions
A is first\(4!=24\)
B is last\(4!=24\)
Both\(3!=6\)

Subtract both forbidden groups, then restore the overlap. \(5!-24-24+6=78\).

As a check, split the allowed rows into \(B\) first and \(B\) in a middle position. \(4!+3\times3\times3!=24+54=78\).

With A not first and B not last, separate B first from B in a middle position. The two cases have different continuation counts.

Restrictions do not usually multiply as independent fractions. Knowing where one card sits can change the available positions of another. Use complete arrangements or disjoint position cases, rather than multiplying two separate “allowed proportions”.

blocks.title: Apply two position restrictions
blocks.prompt: Four distinct cards P, Q, R and S are arranged in a row. First count arrangements with P not first and Q not last. In a separate arrangement problem, fix P in the second position and Q in the last position; count the possibilities.

fields.label: P not first and Q not last

blocks.hint: For the first problem, subtract the arrangements with P first or Q last, adding back their overlap. For the separate fixed-position problem, only two cards remain free.
blocks.solution:
1. \[4!-3!-3!+2!=24-6-6+2=14.\]

    The \(2!\) arrangements with both P first and Q last were otherwise removed twice.

  2. With P second and Q last, R and S fill the two remaining positions in \(2!=2\) ways.

blocks.html:
Exact separation: if exactly \(g\) objects lie between two named objects, their positions differ by \(g+1\). In an otherwise unrestricted row of \(n\ge2\) distinct objects, there are \(n-g-1\) choices for the left position, two orientations of the named objects, then \((n-2)!\) arrangements of the rest:

\[2(n-g-1)(n-2)!,\qquad0\le g\le n-2.\]

The counts are integers. An impossible gap gives zero; if the order of the two named objects is also fixed, omit the factor two.

Relative order: for \(k\) named objects in an unrestricted full row, one specified relative order occurs in \(\frac{n!}{k!}\) arrangements, for integers \(1\le k\le n\). With other restrictions, this division is justified only if swapping those \(k\) labels preserves all the restrictions.

blocks.title: Distinguish an exact separation from relative order
blocks.prompt: Four distinct cards P, Q, R and S are arranged in a row. In one problem, exactly one card must lie between P and Q. In a separate problem, P must occur before Q and Q before R, with no other restriction. Count each set of arrangements.

fields.label: Exactly one card between P and Q

blocks.hint: For the separation, the position pairs are \((1,3)\) and \((2,4)\), with either order of \(\frac{P}{Q}\). For relative order, the six possible orders of P/Q/R occur equally often because no other condition distinguishes them.
blocks.solution:
1. \[2\cdot2\cdot2!=8.\]

    The first factor chooses the two positions, the second their \(\frac{P}{Q}\) orientation, and the final factor arranges R and S.

  2. \[\frac{4!}{3!}=4.\]

    Relative order does not require adjacency: the remaining card may be before, between or after the three ordered cards.

blocks.html:
Block preview: if \(k\) named distinct objects must be consecutive, with no other restriction, treat them as one unit. Arrange the \(n-k+1\) units and then the objects inside the block:

\[(n-k+1)!\,k!,\qquad1\le k\le n.\]

If their internal order is fixed, that block has one internal arrangement instead. The next topic develops blocks, repeated symbols and methods for keeping objects apart.

sections.title: Why do digit questions need separate cases?
sections.label: Digits and leading zero
sections.intro:
A number with a stated number of digits cannot begin with zero. A code may begin with zero only if its rules allow it. Check separately whether digits may repeat.

Fill a restrictive position first when that simplifies the remaining choices. An even number ends in \(0,2,4,6\) or \(8\); a multiple of five ends in \(0\) or \(5\), using only available digits. Without repetition, choosing zero at the end removes no nonzero first-digit option; choosing another even digit does. Split these cases before multiplying.

If the first digit must also lie in a restricted set, check whether each chosen final digit belongs to that set. Only then does it remove a possible first choice.

blocks.html:
Choose the units digit of a four-digit even number formed from \(0,\ldots,6\) with no repeated digits.

Choice counts by position

Units digitThousandsHundredsTensTotal
\(0\)\(6\)\(5\)\(4\)\(1\times6\times5\times4=120\)
\(2,4,6\)\(5\)\(5\)\(4\)\(3\times5\times5\times4=300\)

In the second case the leading digit must avoid both zero and the chosen units digit. \(120+300=420\).

The last digit controls how many nonzero first digits remain. The middle positions are filled after both end digits have been chosen.

blocks.title: Keep the first digit nonzero
blocks.prompt: Use digits \(0,1,2,3,4\) to form three-digit odd numbers. Find the number possible without repeated digits, then the number possible if repetition is allowed.
blocks.hint: The last digit must be \(1\) or \(3\). Choose it first. Then count the nonzero first digits and the available middle digits under each repetition rule.
blocks.solution:
1. Without repetition: two last-digit choices, three remaining nonzero first-digit choices, and three middle-digit choices.

    \[2\cdot3\cdot3=18.\]

  2. With repetition: two last-digit choices, four nonzero first-digit choices, and five middle-digit choices.

    \[2\cdot4\cdot5=40.\]

sections.title: How do counts give probabilities or recover an unknown size?
sections.label: Probabilities and unknown counts
sections.intro:
A counting ratio gives a probability when the complete outcomes in its denominator are equally likely:

\[P(E)=\frac{\text{number of permitted outcomes in }E}{\text{number of outcomes in the sample space}}.\]

If a condition \(F\) is given, restrict both counts to that same condition:

\[P(E\mid F)=\frac{\#(E\cap F)}{\#F},\qquad\#F>0.\]

Here \(\#\) means “number of”. A sequential procedure that chooses among currently available options need not make all valid final arrangements equally likely when different choices have different numbers of completions. Use the sampling rule stated in the question.

blocks.html: For an unknown number of objects, translate the verbal count into products or factorials, state the integer range, then solve. Cancel only factors known to be nonzero. Recheck the original count and every restriction; never round a noninteger solution into a possible stock.

Write the slot product, factorial or case sum before evaluating it on a calculator. Label what each factor counts and why cases do not overlap. For a probability, state the equally likely sample space and apply every given condition to the denominator.

blocks.title: Use the restricted sample space in a conditional probability
blocks.prompt: Six distinct cards P, Q, R, S, T and U are arranged uniformly at random in a row. Given that Q is not last, find the probability that P is first. Enter the count of arrangements satisfying the condition, the count also having P first, and the conditional probability.

fields.label: P first and Q not last

blocks.hint: The denominator counts only arrangements with Q not last. In the numerator fix P first, then remove the arrangements having Q last.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\#(\text{Q not last})=6!-5!=720-120=600.\]
  2. \[\#(\text{P first and Q not last})=5!-4!=120-24=96.\]
  3. \[P(\text{P first}\mid\text{Q not last})=\frac{96}{600}=\frac{4}{25}.\]

    The positive condition count permits this division; using all \(720\) arrangements would answer an unconditional question.

blocks.html: Explore the five-card example below. Turn either forbidden-position rule on or off, inspect the valid labelled rows, and compare the count with all \(120\) equally likely arrangements.

glossary.definition: Objects that can be identified separately; swapping two changes their arrangement.
A specified slot or role, such as first place, last place or secretary, distinguished from the others.
A complete placement of objects in positions where order matters.
For a positive integer \(n\), the product \(n!\) runs from \(n\) down to one; \(0!=1\).
An ordered placement of \(r\) distinct objects chosen without reuse from \(n\); its count is \({}^{n}\mathrm{P}_{r}\).
A symbol may be used again in another position. This changes the available choices.
Cases with no complete outcome in common, so their counts may be added directly.
A named object must occupy one specified slot.
A named object is not allowed in a specified slot; other restrictions still apply.
A specified number of objects lies between two named objects; their position difference is one larger than that number.
Named objects must occur in a specified sequence, without necessarily being adjacent or occupying fixed positions.
A set of objects required to stay consecutive, treated as one unit before its internal order is counted.
Zero in the first position of a digit string; it cannot begin a number of the stated digit length.
Each complete arrangement in the specified sample space has the same probability.

examples.title: Multiply within a case, then add the cases
examples.question: A code has one letter from A, B, C followed by one digit from \(1,2,3,4\). The code C4 is forbidden. How many codes remain?
solution: If the first letter is A or B, all four digits are allowed: \(2\cdot4=8\) codes.
If the letter is C, only three digits are allowed: \(1\cdot3=3\) codes.

\[8+3=11.\]

The cases are disjoint and cover every permitted first letter. As a check, the unrestricted \(3\cdot4=12\) codes lose exactly one forbidden code.

examples.title: Use factorials for a full row and permutations for a shorter row
examples.question: Seven distinct cards A–G are available. Count the ways to arrange all seven in a row, and the ways to fill three labelled display positions without reuse. How many of those three-position displays contain A?
solution:
For the full row, the choices decrease from seven to one:

\[7!=7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=5040.\]

For three positions, make only three choices:

\[{}^{7}\mathrm{P}_{3}=7\cdot6\cdot5=210.\]

The factorial form cancels the unused part of the product:

\[\frac{7!}{(7-3)!}=\frac{7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4!}{4!}=210.\]

If A is required, choose its position, then fill the other two positions from the six remaining cards:

\[3\cdot{}^{6}\mathrm{P}_{2}=3\cdot6\cdot5=90.\]
Do not divide by \(3!\): ABC and BAC are different displays. The four unchosen cards are not arranged anywhere.

examples.title: Fix positions and separate forbidden-position cases
examples.question: Arrange five distinct cards A, B, C, D and E in a row. (a) Count arrangements with A third and B at either end. (b) In a separate problem, count arrangements with A not first and B not last.
solution:
(a) A has one fixed position. Choose either end for B, then arrange the other three cards:

\[2\cdot3!=12.\]

“B at either end” allows two choices; “B last” would allow only one.
(b) If B is first, A is automatically not first. The remaining four cards have \(4!=24\) arrangements.

If B is not first or last, it occupies one of three middle positions. A then has three available positions other than first. The remaining cards have \(3!\) arrangements:

\[3\cdot3\cdot3!=54.\]

\[24+54=78.\]

These B-position cases are disjoint. A second method checks the answer:

\[5!-4!-4!+3!=120-24-24+6=78.\]

Subtract the cases with A first and those with B last, then add back their overlap because it was subtracted twice.

examples.title: Count an exact gap and a specified relative order
examples.question: Six distinct cards A–F are arranged in a row. (a) How many arrangements have exactly two cards between A and B? (b) In a separate problem with no other restrictions, how many arrangements have A before B and B before C?
solution:
(a) The positions of A and B differ by three. The left and right position pairs are \((1,4),(2,5),(3,6)\). Each permits AB or BA, while the other four cards can be arranged freely:

\[3\cdot2\cdot4!=144.\]

(b) A, B and C have \(3!=6\) possible relative orders. Relabelling these three cards takes any one order to any other without breaking a condition, so all six orders occur equally often.

\[\frac{6!}{3!}=120.\]
The second condition fixes only relative order, not positions or adjacency. Do not apply the division by \(3!\) if another restriction treats A, B and C differently.

examples.title: Split the final digit into zero and nonzero cases
examples.question: How many four-digit even numbers can be formed from \(0,1,2,3,4,5,6\) without repeated digits? How many are possible if repetition is allowed instead?
solution:
Without repetition, the final digit is \(0,2,4\) or \(6\). Ending in zero leaves all six nonzero digits available for the first position. The two middle positions then have five and four choices:

\[1\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4=120.\]

Ending in \(2,4\) or \(6\) uses a nonzero digit. For each of these three endings, only five nonzero first digits remain. The middle positions still have five and four choices:

\[3\cdot5\cdot5\cdot4=300.\]

\[120+300=420.\]

The last-digit cases cannot overlap, and every even ending has been included.

With repetition allowed, the first position has six nonzero choices, each middle position has seven choices, and the last has four even choices:

\[6\cdot7\cdot7\cdot4=1176.\]

Repeated digits are permitted in this second experiment; it is not a permutation of distinct cards.

examples.title: Change the denominator when a condition is given
examples.question: The five distinct cards A–E are arranged uniformly at random in a row. Find the probability that A is not first and B is not last. Then find the probability that A is not first given that B is not last.
solution:
All \(5!=120\) arrangements are equally likely. The arrangements meeting both restrictions number

\[5!-4!-4!+3!=78.\]
\[P(\text{A not first and B not last})=\frac{78}{120}=\frac{13}{20}.\]

Given B is not last, restrict the equally likely sample space to

\[5!-4!=96\]

arrangements. Of these, the same \(78\) also have A not first.
\[P(\text{A not first}\mid\text{B not last})=\frac{78}{96}=\frac{13}{16}.\]

examples.title: Recover the number of distinct objects
examples.question: There are \(n\ge3\) distinct objects. The number of ordered arrangements of three objects without reuse is four times the number of ordered arrangements of two objects. Find \(n\).
solution:
Translate the stated counts into descending products:

\[{}^{n}\mathrm{P}_{3}=4\cdot{}^{n}\mathrm{P}_{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n(n-1)(n-2)=4n(n-1).\]

Because \(n\ge3\), the factor \(n(n-1)\) is positive and may be cancelled:

\[n-2=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=6.\]

The answer is an allowed integer. Check the original counts:

\[{}^{6}\mathrm{P}_{3}=120,\qquad{}^{6}\mathrm{P}_{2}=30,\qquad120=4\cdot30.\]

extraPractice.title: A rule changes the number of continuations
extraPractice.prompt: A two-symbol code consists of one letter from A, B, C, D followed by one digit from \(0\) to \(5\). A cannot be followed by \(0\); B must be followed by an even digit, including \(0\). C and D may be followed by any of the six digits. Count all unrestricted codes and the valid codes. If a valid code is chosen uniformly, find the probability that its letter is A.
extraPractice.hint: Split by the first letter. The four cases are disjoint, but have different numbers of permitted digits.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Without restrictions there are \(4\times6=24\) codes.

  2. The continuation counts for A, B, C, D are \(5,3,6,6\). Hence the valid count is \(5+3+6+6=20\).

  3. \[P(\text{A}\mid\text{valid})=\frac{5}{20}=\frac{1}{4}.\]

    Uniform choice among the twenty valid codes justifies this count ratio.

extraPractice.title: A named talk in a partial programme
extraPractice.prompt: There are eight distinct talks, including X. A programme has five ordered places with no repeated talk. Count all programmes, programmes with X first, and programmes containing X anywhere. If all five-talk programmes are equally likely, find the probability that X is included.
extraPractice.hint: For X included, choose its position first and fill the other four places from the seven remaining talks.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[{}^{8}P_5=8\times7\times6\times5\times4=6720.\]

  2. With X first, fill the remaining four places: \({}^{7}P_4=840\).

  3. X has five possible positions. These cases cannot overlap:

    \[5\cdot{}^{7}P_4=4200,\qquad P(\text{X included})=\frac{4200}{6720}=\frac{5}{8}.\]

extraPractice.title: Fix the most restricted places first
extraPractice.prompt: Seven different people, including A and B, stand in a line. Count arrangements with A in an interior position, arrangements with A interior and B fourth, and arrangements with A interior and B at either end. Given a uniformly random arrangement with A interior, find the probability that B is at an end.

fields.label: A interior and B at an end
B at an end given A interior

extraPractice.hint: Interior positions are \(2,3,4,5,6\). Fixing B fourth removes one possible place for A.
extraPractice.solution:
1. A has five interior choices; the others fill the remaining places in \(6!\) ways. This gives \(5(6!)=3600\).

  2. After B is fixed fourth, A has four allowed positions. The remaining five people give \(4(5!)=480\).

  3. Choose one of two ends for B and one of five interior places for A:

    \[2\times5\times5!=1200.\]
  4. \[P(\text{B at an end}\mid\text{A interior})=\frac{1200}{3600}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

extraPractice.title: Divisibility and zero need separate cases
extraPractice.prompt: Five-digit numbers are formed using digits \(0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\) without repetition. Count those ending in zero, those ending in five, and all multiples of five. If a five-digit number from this set is chosen uniformly, find the probability it is a multiple of five. Finally count five-digit multiples of five from the same digits when repetition is allowed.
extraPractice.hint: A multiple of five ends in zero or five. With no repetition, a final five removes one nonzero first-digit choice; a final zero does not.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N_0=7\times6\times5\times4=840,\qquad N_5=6\times6\times5\times4=720.\]

  2. The cases are disjoint, so \(N=840+720=1560\). All permitted five-digit numbers number \(7\times7\times6\times5\times4=5880\).

    \[P(\text{multiple of five})=\frac{1560}{5880}=\frac{13}{49}.\]

  3. With repetition allowed, there are seven nonzero first digits, eight choices for each of the three middle digits, and two final choices:

    \[7\times8^3\times2=7168.\]

extraPractice.title: Distance, adjacency and relative order are different
extraPractice.prompt: Eight distinct cards include A, B and C. Count linear arrangements with exactly two cards between A and B, with A before B before C, and with A adjacent to B. In a uniformly random arrangement, given that A is before B, find the probability that exactly two cards lie between them.

fields.label: Exactly two cards between A and B
Exact gap given A before B

extraPractice.hint: Exactly two cards between A and B means their position numbers differ by three. Relative order allows other cards between the named cards.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The earlier position can be \(1,2,3,4,5\). Choose which of A and B comes first, then arrange the other six cards:

    \[5\times2\times6!=7200.\]

  2. The six relative orders of A, B and C occur equally often in unrestricted rows:

    \[\frac{8!}{3!}=6720.\]

  3. For adjacency, use a block with two internal orders: \(2(7!)=10080\).

  4. Given A before B, there are \(\frac{8!}{2}=20160\) possible rows. The favourable gap count now has only one internal order:

    \[\frac{5(6!)}{20160}=\frac{3600}{20160}=\frac{5}{28}.\]

extraPractice.title: Select and arrange
extraPractice.prompt: From seven different posters choose three. Give the number of selections and the number of ordered displays.
extraPractice.hint: A selection ignores order. Each selection can be displayed in six orders.
extraPractice.solution:
A selection ignores order. Each selection can be displayed in six orders.

  • Selections: \(35\)
  • Ordered displays: \(210\)

extraPractice.title: Treat zero separately
extraPractice.prompt: Use distinct digits from \(\{0,1,2,3,4\}\) to make a three-digit even integer. How many are possible?

retry.feedback: For a nonzero final digit, remove zero from the leading choices.

extraPractice.hint: A final zero leaves four leading choices and three middle choices. A final \(2\) or \(4\) leaves three leading and three middle choices for each ending.
extraPractice.solution:
A final zero leaves four leading choices and three middle choices. A final \(2\) or \(4\) leaves three leading and three middle choices for each ending.

  • Answer: \(30\)

extraPractice.title: Join two neighbours
extraPractice.prompt: Six different pupils stand in a line. How many orders put Amira and Ben together?
extraPractice.hint: Treat the named pair as one unit. Five units can be ordered, with two internal orders for the pair.
extraPractice.solution:
Treat the named pair as one unit. Five units can be ordered, with two internal orders for the pair.

extraPractice.title: Fix a relative order
extraPractice.prompt: Six different books are put in a row. How many orders have the history book somewhere before the geography book?
extraPractice.hint: Swapping the two named books pairs each desired order with one order in which they appear the other way round.
extraPractice.solution:
Swapping the two named books pairs each desired order with one order in which they appear the other way round.

  • Answer: \(360\)

starters.title: Reverse the conditioning event carefully
starters.question: A six-digit number is chosen uniformly from all six-digit numbers formed using \(0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\) without repetition. Let O mean that the number is odd, and H mean that its first digit is greater than \(3\). Find the number of odd numbers and the number satisfying both O and H. Then find \(P(H\mid O)\) and \(P(O\mid H)\).
starters.hint: Count the first and last digits before the four middle places. For the joint event split the final digit into \(1,3\) and \(5,7\), because the latter use up an allowed first digit.
starters.solution:
1. There are four odd final digits. Each leaves six nonzero first choices and six remaining digits for four ordered middle positions:

    \[N(O)=4\times6\times{}^{6}P_4=8640.\]

  2. For O and H, a final \(1\) or \(3\) leaves four high first digits. A final \(5\) or \(7\) leaves only three:

    \[N(O\cap H)=2\times4\times360+2\times3\times360=5040.\]
  3. \[P(H\mid O)=\frac{5040}{8640}=\frac{7}{12}.\]

  4. For H alone, choose the first digit from \(4,5,6,7\), then fill five ordered positions from seven remaining digits:

    \[N(H)=4\cdot{}^{7}P_5=10080,\qquad P(O\mid H)=\frac{5040}{10080}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

    The two conditional probabilities have different denominators.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: exclude a leading zero when counting odd numbers.
  • 1 mark: count the four ordered middle digits correctly.
  • 1 mark: split the joint event into the two disjoint final-digit cases.
  • 1 mark: count both cases with the correct first choices.
  • 1 mark: obtain the joint total.
  • 1 mark: calculate the first conditional with the odd-number denominator.
  • 1 mark: count the conditioning set H.
  • 1 mark: calculate the reversed conditional with its own denominator.

starters.title: Recover the size and combine two restrictions
starters.question:
There are \(n\) distinct objects, including A, B and C, where \(n\ge3\) is an integer. The number of full linear arrangements is \(56\) times the number of full arrangements of a specified set of \(n-2\) of the objects. Find \(n\).

For this value of \(n\), count rows with A before B before C. Also count rows in which A is before B with exactly one object between them. Of these latter rows, how many additionally have C after B? Hence find the conditional probability that C is after B given that A is before B with exactly one object between them, for a uniformly random full row.
starters.hint: Expand only enough of \(n!\) to cancel \((n-2)!\). For the final joint count, let A occupy position \(j\); then B occupies \(j+2\), so the number of places available after B depends on \(j\).
starters.solution:
1. \[n!=56(n-2)!\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n(n-1)=56.\]

    The factorial being cancelled is positive on the stated domain.

    \[(n-8)(n+7)=0.\]

    Only \(n=8\) is an integer in the allowed domain. Check: \(8!=56(6!)\).

  2. In an unrestricted eight-object row, one of the six equally frequent relative orders of A, B and C is allowed:

    \[\frac{8!}{3!}=6720.\]

  3. For exactly one object between A and B with A first, choose A’s position \(j\) from \(1\) to \(6\). B is then fixed at \(j+2\). The remaining six objects can be arranged freely:

    \[6(6!)=4320.\]

  4. If C must also follow B, the available positions for C are \(5,4,3,2,1,0\) as \(j\) runs from \(1\) to \(6\). After choosing C’s position, fill the remaining five places:

    \[(5+4+3+2+1+0)5!=15(120)=1800.\]
  5. \[P(\text{C after B}\mid\text{A before B with one between})=\frac{1800}{4320}=\frac{5}{12}.\]

    The gap restriction breaks the simple three-object relative-order symmetry; count its permitted positions directly.

revision.body:
Define what makes an outcome different. Fill restricted positions first, and count every permitted row once.

When do I multiply, add or subtract?

Multiply when each partial construction has the stated number of continuations. Otherwise split into disjoint cases and add. For forbidden events A and B:

\[N(\text{neither})=N(\text{all})-N(A)-N(B)+N(A\cap B).\]

A number cannot start with zero. For distinct-digit even numbers, separate final zero from other even endings. Check whether repetition is allowed.

Factorials and ordered selections

\[0!=1,\qquad n!=n(n-1)\cdots1,\qquad{}^{n}P_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}.\]

Use nonnegative integers \(n,r\); the product applies for \(n\ge1\). Full rows of distinct objects: \(n!\). For \(r\) ordered places without reuse, require \(0\le r\le n\). To include a named object, choose its position then fill the rest: \(r\cdot{}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\), for \(1\le r\le n\).

Fixed places remove objects and slots. Cancel only nonzero factors; keep valid integer sizes.

Position restrictions, exact gaps and relative order

In a full row of \(n\) distinct objects, exactly \(g\) objects between two names means a position difference of \(g+1\):

\[N=2(n-g-1)(n-2)!,\qquad0\le g\le n-2.\]

Use integers \(n\ge2\) and \(g\). For a prescribed order, omit the factor 2. Adjacency gives \(2(n-1)!\): one block with two internal orders.

A specified relative order of \(m\) named objects in unrestricted rows gives \(\frac{n!}{m!}\), for integers \(1\le m\le n\). Extra restrictions may break the required equal counts for their relative orders.

Use the sample space named in the question

For equally likely elementary arrangements,

\[P(E)=\frac{N(E)}{N(\Omega)},\qquad P(E\mid F)=\frac{N(E\cap F)}{N(F)},\quad N(F)>0.\]

Use matching outcome types. Conditioning changes the denominator. Uniform choices at each local step need not give uniform final valid rows.
revision.checks: • Order, distinctness and repetition stated; leading zero excluded; cases disjoint; every restriction and denominator checked?
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_count_repeated_objects.description: Count arrangements with repeated objects. Update multiplicities when positions are fixed and use blocks or gaps to handle adjacency restrictions.

sections.title: Why do repeated symbols make the count smaller?
sections.label: Repeated visible patterns
sections.intro:
State what makes two outcomes different. Swapping two physical tiles with the same visible letter does not change a visible string. Temporarily label repeated copies, count labelled rows, then divide by the constant number of labellings for each visible row.

If \(n\) symbols have multiplicities \(m_1,\ldots,m_s\), their number of full visible arrangements is

\[\frac{n!}{m_1!m_2!\cdots m_s!},\qquad m_1+\cdots+m_s=n.\]

All multiplicities are nonnegative integers, and \(0!=1\). Use this formula for the specified full multiset; do not apply it unchanged after fixing or omitting a symbol.

blocks.html:
Temporarily distinguish the three identical copies of \(A\) using subscripts.

Six labellings of the same visible row

LabellingRow
\(1\)\(A_1\,B\,A_2\,C\,A_3\,D\,E\)
\(2\)\(A_1\,B\,A_3\,C\,A_2\,D\,E\)
\(3\)\(A_2\,B\,A_1\,C\,A_3\,D\,E\)
\(4\)\(A_2\,B\,A_3\,C\,A_1\,D\,E\)
\(5\)\(A_3\,B\,A_1\,C\,A_2\,D\,E\)
\(6\)\(A_3\,B\,A_2\,C\,A_1\,D\,E\)

All six rows become \(A\,B\,A\,C\,A\,D\,E\) when the labels are removed. Each visible row has this multiplicity, giving \(\frac{7!}{3!}=840\).

Each visible arrangement of AAA and four distinct other letters has exactly six temporary A-labellings. Divide the labelled count by that constant multiplicity.

Only remove distinctions that the outcome ignores. Identical visible copies are interchangeable; different named people, tiles or blocks are not. A division is justified by equal overcounting of every intended outcome.

blocks.title: Divide out each repeated type
blocks.prompt: Arrange the seven symbols X, X, Y, Y, Z, Z and W in a row. Copies of the same letter are indistinguishable. How many different visible strings are possible?
blocks.hint: Temporarily labelling the two copies of each repeated letter creates \(2!\) labellings for each of three types. Every visible string has the same number of such labellings.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N=\frac{7!}{2!\,2!\,2!}=\frac{5040}{8}=630.\]

    Divide by the product of the repetition factorials, not by the number of repeated types.

sections.title: How do fixed positions and number rules change the multiset?
sections.label: Fix symbols before counting
sections.intro: Fix the required visible symbols, subtract those copies from the available multiplicities, then arrange the remainder. If a requirement uses more copies than exist, its count is zero. There is no extra factor for choosing which identical copy occupies a fixed place.

blocks.html: For a number using all given digits, subtract strings with a leading zero. In that subtraction, remove one zero first; the remaining zero multiplicity is one smaller. If an ending is also restricted, split by its digit and update the first-digit calculation within each case. Codes may allow a leading zero if stated.

blocks.title: Remove a zero before counting the invalid strings
blocks.prompt: Use all six digits \(0,0,1,1,4,4\) to form six-digit numbers. Copies of each digit are indistinguishable. How many numbers are possible? If one is selected uniformly, what is the probability that its first digit is \(1\)?
blocks.hint: Count all length-six strings, then subtract strings beginning with zero. Fixing one zero leaves only one zero. For first digit one, fix one copy of one and arrange the remaining multiset.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N(\text{all strings})=\frac{6!}{2!\,2!\,2!}=90.\]
  2. \[N(\text{leading zero})=\frac{5!}{2!\,2!}=30,\qquad N(\text{valid})=90-30=60.\]
  3. \[N(\text{first one})=\frac{5!}{2!\,2!}=30,\qquad P(\text{first one})=\frac{30}{60}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

blocks.html:
Exact separation of two identical symbols: if exactly \(g\) objects must lie between two Xs, their positions differ by \(g+1\). Choose the left position, place both identical Xs, then arrange the remaining multiset. There is no factor of two for swapping the Xs. For example, with XX and distinct B, C, D, exactly one object between the Xs gives three position pairs and \(3!\) remaining orders, hence \(3\cdot3!=18\) strings.

Alternating categories: choose a permitted category pattern first, then fill each category’s places with its own distinct or repeated objects. Category counts differing by more than one make strict alternation impossible. For equal positive counts, either category may start; when counts differ by one, the larger category must occupy both ends.

Relative order with repeats: interpret the statement literally. For “all As before all Bs”, choose the positions occupied by As and Bs, fill those positions with all As followed by all Bs, and arrange the remaining symbols with their multiplicities. For A, A, B, B, C, the \(\frac{A}{B}\) subsequence is AABB; inserting C in its five possible places gives five strings. By contrast, “the first A appears before the first B” permits other \(\frac{A}{B}\) interleavings. For A, A, B, B, B, the first condition allows only AABBB, while the second fixes the first letter as A and permits \(\frac{4!}{3!}=4\) strings. These are different events, so do not automatically divide by two.

sections.title: How do blocks and overlapping conditions combine?
sections.label: Blocks and overlap
sections.intro:
When a specified group must be consecutive, collapse it to one unit, arrange the units, then arrange the contents of each block. Repeated symbols inside a block reduce its internal orders. Repeated units outside a block reduce the external orders only when those whole units are indistinguishable.

For integers \(1\le k\le n\), one prescribed group of \(k\) objects forming a block among \(n\) distinct objects, with no other restriction, gives \((n-k+1)!\,k!\). With repeated symbols, recompute the external unit count and each internal multiset count separately. A prescribed internal order contributes a factor of one.

blocks.html:
For two adjacency events F and G, count their overlap as well as each event:

\[N(\text{at least one})=N(F)+N(G)-N(F\cap G),\]\[N(\text{exactly one})=N(F)+N(G)-2N(F\cap G).\]

Here \(N\) means “number of strings”. Subtract the union from the unrestricted count for neither event.

A block must give one construction for each intended string. Choosing “two of three identical As” creates artificial labels. Allowing an AA block beside the remaining A can also represent AAA in more than one way. Use separate gaps or disjoint run cases when a partial repeated group is involved.

blocks.title: Separate external and internal block orders
blocks.prompt: Arrange A, B, C, X, X and Y in a row. A, B and C must form one consecutive block in any internal order, and the two identical Xs must also be adjacent. Count the strings. Then count them if the ABC block must have that exact internal order.

fields.label: Any internal order of A, B, C

blocks.hint: The units are the three-letter block, the XX block and Y. The XX block has one visible internal arrangement. Decide separately whether the three-letter block has six internal orders or one.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N=3!\cdot3!\cdot1=36.\]

    The two blocks are distinguishable by their contents, even though the two Xs inside one block are identical.

  2. If the three-letter block is fixed as ABC, its internal factor becomes one:

    \[N=3!\cdot1\cdot1=6.\]

sections.title: How do gaps enforce separation and exact runs?
sections.label: Gaps, capacity and runs
sections.intro:
Remove the objects that must be separated. Arrange the remaining \(m\) objects first; every such row has \(m+1\) gap positions, including both ends. The gaps are distinct by their left-to-right positions even when some remaining symbols repeat.

The number of ways to choose \(k\) of \(g\) gaps, ignoring their selection order, is

\[\binom{g}{k}=\frac{g!}{k!(g-k)!},\qquad0\le k\le g,\]

for integers \(g,k\). Put at most one inserted object into each selected gap. Identical inserted objects need no internal ordering; \(k\) distinct inserted objects give an extra \(k!\), or use \(\frac{k!}{s_1!\cdots s_j!}\) for repeated inserted types. This construction enforces that no two inserted objects are adjacent. If \(k>m+1\), the count is zero.

If both ends must be ordinary, only the \(m-1\) internal gaps are usable, for \(m\ge1\). Too few permitted gaps makes the count zero. If distinct inserted objects must follow a fixed relative order, their assignment to the selected left-to-right gaps has only one possibility instead of \(k!\).

blocks.html:
The displayed anchor order is \(B\,C\,D\,E\). Filling gaps \(1,3,5\) gives \(A\,B\,C\,A\,D\,E\,A\).

There are \(4!=24\) anchor orders and \(\binom{5}{3}=10\) gap choices per order. The \(A\)s are identical, giving \(4!\binom{5}{3}=240\) arrangements.

Arrange the four distinct ordinary symbols first, then choose three of their five ordered gap positions for the identical As.

A maximal run is a consecutive group that cannot be extended by another copy of the same symbol. For four identical Rs, two separate RR runs use two different gaps; the two RR blocks are identical, so choose the two gaps without ordering them. A triple and a single use different kinds of blocks, so choose a gap for RRR and then a different gap for R. Four Rs together use one gap. These disjoint run types prevent a long run being counted as several overlapping pairs.

For “no run of three or more”, subtract every forbidden run type, including a four-symbol run if four copies exist. For “not all together”, subtract only the single full block. Those conditions are not interchangeable.

blocks.title: Read the exact adjacency condition
blocks.prompt: Arrange A, A, A, B and C, with the As indistinguishable. Count strings with no adjacent As, strings where the three As are not all together, and strings with exactly one adjacent AA pair but no AAA run. Finally, can four identical As be placed with B and C so that no two As are adjacent? Enter its count.

fields.label: Exactly one AA pair, with the other A isolated

blocks.hint: B and C have two orders, each with three gaps. Distinguish choosing three gaps for single As from choosing one gap for AA and another for A. A fourth isolated A would need a fourth gap.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N(\text{all strings})=\frac{5!}{3!}=20,\qquad N(\text{AAA together})=3!=6.\]
  2. \[N(\text{no AA})=2!\binom{3}{3}=2.\]
  3. \[N(\text{not all together})=20-6=14.\]
  4. \[N(\text{exactly one AA pair})=2!\cdot3\cdot2=12.\]

    The pair gap and the single-A gap must be different.

  5. With only B and C as separators there are three gaps. Four isolated As cannot fit, so the count is zero.

blocks.html: The model uses the smaller set consisting of identical As and distinct B, C. With two ordinary symbols there are only three gaps. Compare two, three and four As, then switch between all strings, one full A block and no adjacent As.

sections.title: What changes when a tile is omitted or a string is chosen randomly?
sections.label: Partial displays and probability
sections.intro: For a shorter visible display, split by the numbers of each symbol that are actually used. Count the arrangements of each feasible remaining multiset, then add these disjoint cases. When exactly one tile is omitted, splitting by the omitted symbol type is enough; do not multiply by the number of identical copies of that type.

blocks.html:
Probability needs a stated sampling model. Under a uniform choice of distinct visible full strings, use favourable strings divided by all permitted strings. A uniform shuffle of every physical tile gives the same visible-string distribution because every full string has the same product of multiplicity factorials as its number of labelled versions. This also holds when exactly one tile is omitted: the omitted symbol type is uniquely recoverable from the displayed counts.

Shorter physical samples need not be uniform over visible strings. From A, A, B, C, drawing two physical tiles in order without replacement gives \({}^{4}\mathrm{P}_{2}=12\) equally likely labelled outcomes. AA has two labelled outcomes, but BC has only one. Their probabilities are \(\frac{1}{6}\) and \(\frac{1}{12}\), not equal visible-string probabilities.

For a conditional probability under a uniform visible-string model, restrict both counts to the given condition, whose count must be positive. Choosing uniformly among the remaining symbol types at each step is another process and need not generate uniform final strings.

State what is counted: labelled physical arrangements, distinct visible strings or valid numbers. Identify each block and each repetition factor. For an omitted symbol or a conditional event, update both the multiplicities and the sample-space count before dividing.

blocks.title: Omit one symbol type, without labelling identical copies
blocks.prompt: From P, P, Q, Q, Q, R and R, form a visible six-symbol string by omitting one tile and arranging the other six. Count all distinct strings and those with a Q omitted. In a separate probability experiment, the seven physical tiles are shuffled uniformly and the last tile is removed. Find the probability that the omitted tile is a Q.

fields.label: Probability the omitted tile is Q

blocks.hint: Split by the omitted symbol type P, Q or R. Count each remaining multiset once. Omitting one of three identical Qs does not create three different visible strings.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N_P=\frac{6!}{3!\,2!}=60,\qquad N_Q=\frac{6!}{2!\,2!\,2!}=90,\qquad N_R=\frac{6!}{2!\,3!}=60.\]
  2. \[N=60+90+60=210.\]

  3. Exactly one tile is omitted. Each visible six-symbol string has the same \(2!\,3!\,2!\) labellings in the physical shuffle, so the string count ratio is valid:

    \[P(\text{omit Q})=\frac{90}{210}=\frac{3}{7}.\]

    This also follows directly because three of the seven physical tiles are Qs.

glossary.definition: Copies whose exchange does not change the visible outcome being counted.
A collection recording both the symbol types and how many copies of each are available.
The number of copies of a particular symbol in the current collection.
An artificial mark used to count physical arrangements before equal visible outcomes are grouped together.
A prescribed consecutive group treated as one external unit before its internal visible orders are counted.
The arrangement of the symbols inside a block.
A position between consecutive ordinary objects or at an allowed end where an inserted object or run can be placed.
A consecutive group of one symbol type that cannot be extended by another adjacent copy of that type.
No two of the specified objects or symbols are adjacent; this is stronger than saying they are not all together.
An ordered visible string using only some of the available tiles.
Every permitted visible string has the same probability; this must be stated or justified from the physical sampling model.

examples.title: Count visible rows rather than temporary labels
examples.question: Arrange A, A, A, B, C, D and E in a row, treating the three As as identical. Find the number of different visible strings.
solution: Temporarily distinguish the As as \(A_1,A_2,A_3\). All seven labelled objects have \(7!=5040\) arrangements.
Every visible string has exactly \(3!=6\) labelled versions, obtained by permuting the labels on its three A positions. This multiplicity does not depend on the positions.

\[N=\frac{7!}{3!}=840.\]

No factorial is needed for B, C, D or E because each appears once.

examples.title: Reduce the multiplicities after fixing positions
examples.question: Use all of A, A, A, B, C, D and E. How many visible strings start with A? How many have A at both ends?
solution:
Fixing A first leaves two As and four distinct other symbols:

\[N(\text{first A})=\frac{6!}{2!}=360.\]

Fixing A at both ends leaves one A and B, C, D, E. All five remaining symbols are distinct:

\[N(\text{both ends A})=5!=120.\]
There is no factor of three for choosing which A is first. The visible outcome does not distinguish the identical copies.

examples.title: Exclude leading zero with the reduced multiset
examples.question: Form seven-digit numbers using all digits \(0,0,1,2,2,3,4\). Count the valid numbers and those beginning with \(2\). If a valid number is selected uniformly, find the probability it begins with \(2\).
solution:
Ignoring the first-digit restriction, the distinct strings number

\[\frac{7!}{2!\,2!}=1260.\]

Fixing one zero first leaves one zero, two twos and the other three distinct digits. The invalid strings number

\[\frac{6!}{2!}=360.\]

Hence there are \(1260-360=900\) valid seven-digit numbers.

Fixing one two first leaves two zeros, one two and three other distinct digits:

\[N(\text{first two})=\frac{6!}{2!}=360.\]

\[P(\text{first two})=\frac{360}{900}=\frac{2}{5}.\]

The denominator contains valid seven-digit numbers, not strings with a leading zero.

examples.title: Count a repeated block and two separate required blocks
examples.question: (a) Arrange A, A, A, B, C, D and E with all three As together. (b) In a separate problem, arrange A, A, B, C, C, D and E so that A, A, B form one consecutive block in any order and C, C form another consecutive block.
solution:
(a) The units are AAA, B, C, D and E. These five units are distinct. The identical letters inside AAA have only one visible order:

\[N=5!\cdot1=120.\]
(b) The four units are the AAB block, the CC block, D and E. Their external order has \(4!\) possibilities.

The first block has \(\frac{3!}{2!}=3\) internal orders: AAB, ABA and BAA. The CC block has one. Therefore

\[N=4!\cdot\frac{3!}{2!}\cdot1=72.\]
Do not divide the four-unit count by \(2!\): the two blocks have different contents. Repetition inside a block is handled in its internal factor.

examples.title: Correct the overlap between two adjacent-pair events
examples.question: Arrange A, A, B, B, C, D and E. Let F mean that the As are adjacent and G mean that the Bs are adjacent. Count strings with both events, at least one event, exactly one event, and neither event.
solution:
\[N(\text{all})=\frac{7!}{2!\,2!}=1260.\]

For F, collapse AA into one unit; the two Bs remain identical. The same reasoning applies to G:

\[N(F)=N(G)=\frac{6!}{2!}=360.\]

For both events, the units AA, BB, C, D and E are distinct:

\[N(F\cap G)=5!=120.\]

\[N(F\cup G)=360+360-120=600.\]

The overlap was counted twice in the sum and must be retained once.

\[N(\text{exactly one})=360+360-2(120)=480.\]

Neither event occurs in \(1260-600=660\) strings. The three categories neither, exactly one and both check the total: \(660+480+120=1260\).

examples.title: Choose separate gaps for a pair and a single symbol
examples.question: Arrange A, A, A, B, C, D and E. Count strings with no adjacent As, with exactly one adjacent AA pair and an isolated A, and with the three As not all together. If a visible full string is chosen uniformly, also find the probability of no adjacent As given that they are not all together.
solution: First arrange B, C, D and E in \(4!=24\) ways. Every such row has five gaps, including the two ends.

For no adjacent As, choose three different gaps. Identical As need no further ordering:

\[N(\text{no AA})=4!\binom{5}{3}=24\cdot10=240.\]

For exactly one AA pair, choose one of five gaps for the pair and a different one of four gaps for the single A:

\[N(\text{one pair})=4!\cdot5\cdot4=480.\]

Using the same gap would create AAA. There is no choice of which two physical As form the visible pair.

All three As form one block in \(5!=120\) strings. Thus

\[N(\text{not all together})=840-120=720.\]

This includes both the \(240\) fully separated strings and the \(480\) strings with one pair. “Not all together” is weaker than “no two adjacent”.

If a distinct visible full string is chosen uniformly, the probability of no adjacent As, given that they are not all together, is

\[\frac{240}{720}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

examples.title: Omit one tile by its symbol type
examples.question: From A, A, A, B, C, D and E, omit one tile and arrange the other six. Count the distinct visible six-symbol strings. If all seven physical tiles are shuffled uniformly and the last one is removed, find the probability that an A was omitted.
solution:
If an A is omitted, the remaining multiset has two As and four distinct other letters:

\[N_A=\frac{6!}{2!}=360.\]

If B, C, D or E is omitted, the remaining multiset has three As and three other distinct letters. Each omitted ordinary type gives

\[\frac{6!}{3!}=120\]

strings. These four omitted-type cases are separate.

\[N=360+4(120)=840.\]

Do not multiply the A-omission count by three: it would count every visible string three times.

From any six-symbol string, the missing symbol type is uniquely determined. Appending that symbol gives one full visible seven-symbol string. Each shorter string matches exactly one full string, so the same constant \(3!\) labelling multiplicity applies to the physical-shuffle experiment.

\[P(\text{A omitted})=\frac{360}{840}=\frac{3}{7}.\]
