extraPractice.title: Fix a repeated letter and recount the remainder
extraPractice.prompt: The symbols A, A, A, B, B, C, C, D are arranged in a line; equal letters are indistinguishable. Count all distinct patterns, those beginning with A, and those with neither end A. For a pattern chosen uniformly from all distinct patterns, find the probability that its last letter is not A given that its first letter is A.

fields.label: Last not A given first A

extraPractice.hint: Remove each fixed A before writing the remaining repeated-letter factorials. For neither end A, subtract the two end events and restore their overlap.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N=\frac{8!}{3!2!2!}=1680,\qquad N(\text{first A})=\frac{7!}{2!2!2!}=630.\]

  2. The same count applies to last A. With both ends A, only one A remains:

    \[N(\text{both ends A})=\frac{6!}{2!2!}=180.\]
  3. \[N(\text{neither end A})=1680-630-630+180=600.\]

  4. Within the first-A patterns, \(630-180=450\) do not end in A:

    \[P(\text{last not A}\mid\text{first A})=\frac{450}{630}=\frac{5}{7}.\]

extraPractice.title: Exactly one pair differs from at least one pair
extraPractice.prompt: Arrange A, A, B, B, C, D, E, F in a row. Equal letters are indistinguishable. Let U mean that the two As are adjacent, and V mean that the two Bs are adjacent. Count patterns satisfying both U and V, exactly one of U and V, and at least one of them. For a uniformly chosen distinct pattern, find the probability of exactly one given at least one.

fields.label: Exactly one given at least one

extraPractice.hint: AA and BB each have only one internal pattern. Count their intersection using two distinct blocks. Exactly-one removes the intersection twice from the sum of the two event counts.
extraPractice.solution:
1. With AA as one block, the two Bs are still identical. Thus

    \[N(U)=\frac{7!}{2!}=2520,\qquad N(V)=2520.\]

  2. With both blocks formed, six distinct units remain:

    \[N(U\cap V)=6!=720.\]
  3. \[N(\text{exactly one})=2520+2520-2(720)=3600.\]
  4. \[N(\text{at least one})=2520+2520-720=4320,\qquad P=\frac{3600}{4320}=\frac{5}{6}.\]

    The distinction concerns which pair-events occur, not hidden identities of the equal letters.

extraPractice.title: Choose gaps for identical counters
extraPractice.prompt: Five different numbered counters and three identical red counters are arranged in a line. Count patterns with no adjacent reds; patterns with no adjacent reds and a numbered counter at each end; patterns with exactly one red pair and the third red separate; and patterns with all three reds consecutive.

fields.label: No adjacent reds and numbered ends
One red pair and a separate single red

extraPractice.hint: Arrange the five numbered counters first. There are six gaps including the ends, but only four internal gaps. A pair-gap and a single-gap have different roles.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N(\text{no adjacent reds})=5!\binom{6}{3}=120(20)=2400.\]

  2. If both ends must be numbered, use only the four internal gaps:

    \[5!\binom{4}{3}=480.\]

  3. For exactly one pair, choose its gap and then a different gap for the single red:

    \[5!\times6\times5=3600.\]

  4. For a triple, treat RRR as one unit: \(6!=720\). The unrestricted total is \(\frac{8!}{3!}=6720\), and \(2400+3600+720=6720\). These three run types are disjoint and exhaustive.

extraPractice.title: Distinct special objects have internal orders
extraPractice.prompt: Five different ordinary objects and four different special objects M, N, P, Q are arranged in one line. Count rows in which all four special objects are consecutive, rows in which no two special objects are adjacent, and rows in which the four special objects are not all consecutive. Finally count rows with no adjacent special objects in which their left-to-right order is M, N, P, Q.

fields.label: Separated with the specified relative order

extraPractice.hint: A four-object block has \(4!\) internal orders. For separation, five ordinary objects leave six gaps. With a fixed relative order, choosing the four gaps fixes which special object occupies each.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The block and five ordinary objects form six distinct units:

    \[6!\,4!=17280.\]

  2. Arrange the ordinary objects, choose four different gaps, then assign the four specials:

    \[5!\binom{6}{4}4!=43200.\]

  3. “Not all consecutive” is the complement of the four-object block event:

    \[9!-17280=345600.\]

    It permits two or three specials to be adjacent, so it is not the no-adjacency event.

  4. With the relative order fixed, each four-gap choice has just one assignment:

    \[5!\binom{6}{4}=1800.\]

extraPractice.title: Omit a symbol type without creating hidden labels
extraPractice.prompt: Available tiles show A, A, A, B, B, C, D. Display six of the seven tiles in order, leaving exactly one unused. Equal letters are indistinguishable, and only the displayed string matters. Count all distinct six-letter strings, those omitting an A, and those beginning with A. A distinct displayed string is then chosen uniformly; find the probability it begins with A given that an A was omitted.

fields.label: First A given an A omitted

extraPractice.hint: Split by the omitted letter type A, B, C or D. A displayed string determines that omitted type. Do not multiply the omitted-A case by three: the As have no visible labels.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\begin{aligned}N(\text{omit A})&=\frac{6!}{2!2!}=180,\\N(\text{omit B})&=\frac{6!}{3!}=120,\\N(\text{omit C})=N(\text{omit D})&=\frac{6!}{3!2!}=60.\end{aligned}\]

  2. The cases are disjoint, giving \(180+120+60+60=420\).

  3. For first A, remove that A within each omission case. The four counts are

    \[\frac{5!}{2!}=60,\quad\frac{5!}{2!}=60,\quad\frac{5!}{2!2!}=30,\quad\frac{5!}{2!2!}=30.\]

    Thus \(180\) strings begin with A.

  4. Of the \(180\) strings omitting A, \(60\) begin with A:

    \[P(\text{first A}\mid\text{omit A})=\frac{60}{180}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

    The two As left in the six-letter display occupy two of its six positions.

extraPractice.title: Recount after fixing a letter
extraPractice.prompt: How many distinct arrangements of BALLOON begin with L?
extraPractice.hint: One L is already fixed. In the remaining six letters only the two O symbols are identical.
extraPractice.solution:
One L is already fixed. In the remaining six letters only the two O symbols are identical.

  • Answer: \(360\)

extraPractice.title: Count just one paired run
extraPractice.prompt: Arrange AABB. How many distinct arrangements have exactly one of the pairs AA and BB adjacent?
extraPractice.hint: There are three orders for each pair-block event and two orders with both pairs adjacent. Each of the two separate events therefore contributes one order.
extraPractice.solution:
There are three orders for each pair-block event and two orders with both pairs adjacent. Each of the two separate events therefore contributes one order.

  • Answer: \(2\)

extraPractice.title: Separate identical counters
extraPractice.prompt: Arrange four distinct blue counters and two identical red counters in a row. How many orders keep the red counters apart?
extraPractice.hint: Order the blue counters first. They create five gaps, of which any two can each receive one red counter.
extraPractice.solution:
Order the blue counters first. They create five gaps, of which any two can each receive one red counter.

  • Answer: \(240\)

extraPractice.title: Choose different gaps
extraPractice.prompt: Arrange three different blue counters and three identical red counters. How many orders have a red pair and a separate single red counter?
extraPractice.hint: There are four gaps after ordering the blue counters. Choose the gap for the pair and a different gap for the single.
extraPractice.solution:
There are four gaps after ordering the blue counters. Choose the gap for the pair and a different gap for the single.

  • Answer: \(72\)

starters.title: Repeated zeros interact with both end conditions
starters.question: Use every digit in the multiset \(0,0,1,1,2,3\) exactly once to form a six-digit number. Count all distinct six-digit numbers, the even numbers, and the even numbers with no adjacent zeros. A number is selected uniformly from the valid six-digit numbers. Find the probability that its zeros are separated given that it is even.
starters.hint: Subtract strings beginning with zero. For even numbers split the final digit into zero or two. For separated zeros, identify their allowed positions separately in those two cases.
starters.solution:
1. Count all six-symbol strings and subtract those beginning with zero:

    \[\frac{6!}{2!2!}-\frac{5!}{2!}=180-60=120.\]

  2. Ending in zero leaves one zero and two ones. Exclude a leading zero:

    \[N_0=\frac{5!}{2!}-\frac{4!}{2!}=48.\]

  3. Ending in two leaves two zeros and two ones:

    \[N_2=\frac{5!}{2!2!}-\frac{4!}{2!}=18.\]

    There are \(48+18=66\) even numbers.

  4. With a zero last, the other zero may occupy position \(2,3\) or \(4\): position \(1\) is forbidden and position \(5\) would make the zeros adjacent. Fill the other four positions with \(1,1,2,3\):

    \[3\cdot \frac{4!}{2!}=36.\]

  5. With two last, the nonadjacent zero-position pairs among positions \(2,3,4,5\) are \((2,4),(2,5),(3,5)\). Fill the other three positions with \(1,1,3\):

    \[3\cdot \frac{3!}{2!}=9.\]
  6. \[N(\text{even and separated zeros})=36+9=45,\qquad P=\frac{45}{66}=\frac{15}{22}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: remove leading-zero strings from the full multiset count.
  • 1 mark: split the even case by its final digit.
  • 1 mark: obtain the valid final-zero count.
  • 1 mark: obtain the valid final-two count and even total.
  • 1 mark: find the allowable location of the other zero when zero is last.
  • 1 mark: find the three nonadjacent zero-position pairs when two is last.
  • 1 mark: obtain the combined separated-zero count.
  • 1 mark: divide by the even-number conditioning count.

starters.title: Two identical pair-blocks must not be ordered twice
starters.question: Four distinct numbered counters and four identical red counters are arranged in a line. A red run is a maximal consecutive group of red counters. Count patterns with exactly two red runs, both of length two; patterns containing a red run of length at least three; and patterns with no red run longer than two. For a uniformly chosen distinct pattern, find the probability of two red runs of length two given that no run is longer than two.
starters.hint: Arrange the four numbered counters, making five gaps. Two RR blocks are identical and must occupy distinct gaps. For a run of at least three, separate the possibilities RRR plus R and RRRR.
starters.solution:
1. Choose two of the five gaps for the identical RR blocks. A numbered counter separates distinct gaps:

    \[4!\binom{5}{2}=240.\]

    Do not multiply by \(2!\): interchanging identical RR blocks creates no new pattern.

  2. A triple and a single must use different gaps. Their roles differ, so choose the triple-gap and then the single-gap:

    \[4!\times5\times4=480.\]

  3. An RRRR block gives \(5!=120\) patterns. These are disjoint from the triple-plus-single case, so the long-run count is \(480+120=600\).

  4. The unrestricted multiset count is \(\frac{8!}{4!}=1680\). Therefore the no-longer-than-two count is \(1680-600=1080\).

  5. \[P(\text{two length-two runs}\mid\text{no run longer than two})=\frac{240}{1080}=\frac{2}{9}.\]

    A triple has two adjacent red-red boundaries, but it is not two separated length-two runs. The prompt’s run definition matters.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: arrange the ordinary counters and identify five gaps.
  • 1 mark: choose two gaps without labelling the identical pair-blocks.
  • 1 mark: count triple-plus-single patterns in distinct gaps.
  • 1 mark: count four-red blocks and combine the disjoint long-run cases.
  • 1 mark: count the unrestricted multiset patterns.
  • 1 mark: obtain the no-longer-than-two conditioning count.
  • 1 mark: calculate the conditional probability using the defined run event.

revision.body:
Count visible patterns once. Decide which objects and blocks are distinguishable before multiplying.

Repeated symbols and fixed positions

For multiplicities \(a,b,\ldots\) totalling \(n\), all nonnegative integers,

\[N=\frac{n!}{a!b!\cdots},\qquad0!=1.\]

Remove fixed symbols and recount remaining multiplicities. For numbers, subtract leading-zero strings. Exactly two copies of one symbol with \(g\) objects between them use \(n-g-1\) position pairs, for \(0\le g\le n-2\), without an orientation factor. Arrange the remaining multiset.

Blocks and overlapping pair-events

Arrange outer units, then their distinct internal patterns. A block of \(k\) distinct objects among \(n\) distinct objects gives \((n-k+1)!k!\), for integers \(1\le k\le n\). Identical-symbol blocks have one internal pattern; identical blocks are unlabelled.

For pair-events with counts \(e,f\) and intersection count \(h\):

\[N(\text{at least one})=e+f-h,\qquad N(\text{exactly one})=e+f-2h.\]

“Not all together” complements the whole-block event; smaller adjacent groups remain allowed.

Choose gaps, then assign the inserted objects

Arrange \(q\) distinct ordinary objects: \(q!\) ways and \(q+1\) gaps including the ends. For \(m\) separated special objects:

\[N_{\text{identical}}=q!\binom{q+1}{m},\qquad N_{\text{distinct}}=q!\binom{q+1}{m}m!.\]

Require integers \(q\ge0\), \(0\le m\le q+1\); excess objects cannot fit. Ordinary ends permit only \(q-1\) internal gaps, for \(q\ge1\).

For three identical reds, exactly one pair uses a pair-gap and a different single-gap: \(q!(q+1)q\). A triple is separate. Two identical RR blocks use an unordered pair of gaps. A run is a maximal consecutive group.

Partial displays and probabilities

Split shorter displays by retained multiplicities or omitted symbol types, then add disjoint counts. Do not label identical copies.

\[P(E\mid F)=\frac{N(E\cap F)}{N(F)},\qquad N(F)>0.\]

Shorter physical draws may weight visible strings unequally. This count ratio requires equally likely outcomes and matching sample spaces.
revision.checks: • Check remaining copies, allowed gaps, block identities, runs and the sampling model.
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_count_selections.description: Use combinations to count selections under restrictions. Distinguish picking members from assigning roles and identify equally likely outcomes.

sections.title: When is a selection unordered?
sections.label: Combinations and order
sections.intro:
A committee is determined by its members, not by the order in which they were chosen. People remain distinct even when they share the same category. Selecting A, B and C gives the same committee as selecting C, A and B; assigning them to different named roles can give different outcomes.

Each unordered selection of \(r\) distinct objects has exactly \(r!\) ordered lists. Dividing the ordered count by this constant gives

\[\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!},\qquad n,r\in\mathbb{Z},\quad0\le r\le n.\]

Here \(n!=n(n-1)\cdots1\) for positive integers, and \(0!=1\). There is one empty selection and one selection of the whole pool: \(\binom{n}{0}=\binom{n}{n}=1\). Choosing more than the available objects is impossible and contributes zero; do not evaluate a negative factorial. Also \(\binom{n}{r}=\binom{n}{n-r}\), because choosing the included set determines the omitted set.

After choosing \(r\) members, one chair contributes \(r\) choices; two different officers contribute \(r(r-1)\), provided \(r\ge2\). More generally, assign different roles to distinct selected members by an ordered-slot count.

blocks.html:
Three people are chosen from eight. Only their membership is recorded.

Six orders of one committee

ListingMembers in listing order
\(1\)\(P_2,P_5,P_7\)
\(2\)\(P_2,P_7,P_5\)
\(3\)\(P_5,P_2,P_7\)
\(4\)\(P_5,P_7,P_2\)
\(5\)\(P_7,P_2,P_5\)
\(6\)\(P_7,P_5,P_2\)

Every committee has \(3!=6\) orders. There are \(\frac{8\times7\times6}{3!}=\binom{8}{3}=56\) committees.

All six orders of the same three people collapse to one committee. The division works because every committee has exactly six ordered versions.

Describe the final outcome first. A set of members, a set with one chair, and an assignment to several different roles are different objects to count. Divide only by an overcount that is the same for every intended outcome.

blocks.title: Decide what makes two outcomes different
blocks.prompt: Seven distinct pupils are available. Count three-person committees, committees with one selected member appointed chair, and appointments to three different named roles. No pupil can hold more than one role.
blocks.hint: A committee ignores the order in which its members were selected. One chair gives three choices within each committee. Three different roles distinguish all six orders of its members.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N(\text{committee})=\binom{7}{3}=35.\]
  2. \[N(\text{committee and chair})=3\binom{7}{3}=105.\]
  3. \[N(\text{three roles})=7\cdot6\cdot5=210.\]

    The role assignment, not the word “choose”, determines whether order matters.

sections.title: How do exact and at-least compositions differ?
sections.label: Composition cases
sections.intro:
For two disjoint categories containing \(a\) and \(b\) distinct people, an \(r\)-person selection, with \(0\le r\le a+b\), containing exactly \(j\) from the first category has

\[\binom{a}{j}\binom{b}{r-j}\]

possibilities. Its feasible integer counts satisfy

\[\max(0,r-b)\le j\le\min(a,r).\]

For “at least”, add the counts of every allowed exact composition, or subtract its complement from the unrestricted count. Multiply choices within a fixed disjoint-category construction; add separate composition cases. Neither operation follows from a keyword alone.

blocks.html:
Choose four people from four new and five experienced members.

Composition of the committee

NewExperiencedSelectionsCount
\(0\)\(4\)\(\binom{4}{0}\binom{5}{4}\)\(5\)
\(1\)\(3\)\(\binom{4}{1}\binom{5}{3}\)\(40\)
\(2\)\(2\)\(\binom{4}{2}\binom{5}{2}\)\(60\)
\(3\)\(1\)\(\binom{4}{3}\binom{5}{1}\)\(20\)
\(4\)\(0\)\(\binom{4}{4}\binom{5}{0}\)\(1\)

The disjoint counts sum to \(\binom{9}{4}=126\). At least two new members gives \(60+20+1=81\).

Five experienced and four new people give five possible compositions of a four-person committee. Each committee belongs to exactly one composition case.

Do not designate a qualifying member unless that designation is part of the outcome. Choosing one new person first and then three other people gives \(4\binom{8}{3}=224\) constructions for the main pool. A committee with \(k\) new members is counted \(k\) times. The actual number with at least one new member is \(\binom{9}{4}-\binom{5}{4}=121\); no fixed division repairs the varying overcount.

For three disjoint categories, list the allowed count triples first. Each triple must total the committee size and stay within each category’s capacity. Multiply its three combination counts, then add the allowed triples. If the chair must come from one category, multiply each composition count by the number of selected members eligible to chair; that factor can vary between compositions.

blocks.title: List the allowed three-category compositions
blocks.prompt: A pool contains three programmers, four designers and two analysts; these categories are disjoint and everyone is distinct. Select four people with exactly one analyst and more designers than programmers. Count the committees. Then count the outcomes if a designer on the committee must be appointed chair.
blocks.hint: After selecting one analyst, the remaining \(\text{(designer, programmer)}\) counts are \((3,0)\) or \((2,1)\). The number of eligible chairs differs between these cases.
blocks.solution:
1. The allowed compositions are \((D,P,A)=(3,0,1)\) and \((2,1,1)\).

    \[N=\binom{2}{1}\binom{4}{3}\binom{3}{0}+\binom{2}{1}\binom{4}{2}\binom{3}{1}=8+36=44.\]

  2. The first case has three eligible chairs per committee; the second has two:

    \[N(\text{with chair})=3(8)+2(36)=96.\]

    Do not multiply the whole committee count by one fixed number of designers.

sections.title: How do named people and complete pairs change the choices?
sections.label: Named members and pairs
sections.intro:
Reserve required people, remove forbidden people, then fill the remaining places. If \(q\) required people and \(f\) forbidden people are distinct disjoint sets in a pool of \(n\), the count is \(\binom{n-q-f}{r-q}\), provided the remaining quota is feasible. A person cannot be both required and forbidden. Within a category, reduce both its available count and its remaining quota after reserving a member.

For two named people, “not both” includes exactly one or neither; “at least one” includes exactly one or both. “Both or neither” is an all-or-none rule. For any specified nonempty set, count its all-included and all-excluded cases separately; add them because those cases cannot overlap.

blocks.title: Separate both, neither and exactly one
blocks.prompt: Select three people from six distinct people, including the named people P and Q. Count committees containing both P and Q, committees containing exactly one of them, and committees satisfying the rule “include both or include neither”.

fields.label: Exactly one of P and Q

blocks.hint: Once P and Q are reserved, one place remains. For neither, choose all three members from the other four. Exactly one has two separate named-person cases.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N(\text{both})=\binom{4}{1}=4.\]
  2. \[N(\text{exactly one})=2\binom{4}{2}=12.\]
  3. \[N(\text{both or neither})=\binom{4}{1}+\binom{4}{3}=4+4=8.\]

    The three disjoint categories check the total: \(4+12+4=20=\binom{6}{3}\).

blocks.html:
For specified pairs, decide how many pairs must be complete. Choose those pairs first. Then choose the other represented pairs and one member from each, so no extra complete pair is accidentally formed. For a pool of \(2m\) distinct people partitioned into \(m\) disjoint specified pairs, an \(r\)-person selection containing exactly \(k\) complete pairs has

\[\binom{m}{k}\binom{m-k}{r-2k}\,2^{r-2k}\]

possibilities when \(m,r,k\) are nonnegative integers, \(k\le m\) and \(0\le r-2k\le m-k\); otherwise that composition is impossible. The powers of two choose which member represents each incomplete pair.

sections.title: What if the categories overlap?
sections.label: Overlapping categories
sections.intro:
Separate the population into four disjoint regions: first category only, second category only, both, and neither. Then choose physical people from those regions. A person in the overlap may satisfy both skill requirements while occupying just one place.

You can add disjoint region-composition cases. Alternatively, count all committees, subtract those missing the first requirement and those missing the second, then add back those missing both. That last set was subtracted twice. Check whether the problem allows members with neither skill; “both skills represented” does not mean every member must belong to their union.

blocks.html: Write the counting expression before evaluating it. A short region table or composition list shows what each factor means. Check that the cases cover the event once each and that their total cannot exceed the unrestricted count.

blocks.title: Keep the overlapping membership cell intact
blocks.prompt: Eight people comprise two who have only music skills, two who have only sport skills, one who has both, and three who have neither. Select two distinct people. How many selections have both skills represented? How many of these selections contain no person with both skills?

fields.label: Both skills, without a dual-skilled member

blocks.hint: If the dual-skilled person is selected, the other person can be any of the seven others. If that person is excluded, the two members must be one music-only and one sport-only person.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N(\text{with dual-skilled person})=1\cdot7=7.\]
  2. \[N(\text{without dual-skilled person})=\binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{1}=4.\]
  3. \[N(\text{both skills})=7+4=11.\]

    One person can supply both skills, but cannot fill two places in the selection.

sections.title: Which selection outcomes are equally likely?
sections.label: Probabilities and unknown counts
sections.intro:
If every physical \(r\)-person subset of a distinct \(n\)-person pool is equally likely, the probability of an event is its valid subset count divided by \(\binom{n}{r}\). Given a condition H with at least one valid subset, restrict both counts to H:

\[P(C\mid H)=\frac{N(C\cap H)}{N(H)},\qquad N(H)>0.\]

For the earlier pool, given that \(N_1\) is included and \(N_2\) excluded, the probability of exactly two new people is \(\frac{20}{35}=\frac{4}{7}\). The unrestricted denominator \(126\) would answer a different question. Uniformly choosing a composition and then its members does not generally make all committees equally likely.

blocks.html: The model below uses a separate smaller pool: three new and three experienced people, choosing three. Compare the joint probability in all twenty committees with the conditional probability inside the selected named rules.

Repeated letter types need a separate sample space. For unordered visible selections, list feasible multiplicity vectors: retained counts are integers, sum to the sample size, and cannot exceed the available copies. For uniform physical-tile subsets, a type vector \((j_1,\ldots,j_s)\) has \(\prod_{i=1}^{s}\binom{a_i}{j_i}\) physical versions when type \(i\) has \(a_i\) available copies. The product symbol means to multiply one combination factor for each letter type. Those multiplicities can differ between visible types.

blocks.title: Distinguish a letter type from a physical subset
blocks.prompt: The five physical tiles are A, A, B, B and C. Select two tiles. First count the possible unordered letter-type selections, ignoring which identical copy was used. In a separate experiment, a physical two-tile subset is selected uniformly. Find the probability of type AB and the probability that an A is selected given that C is selected.

fields.label: Probability of an A given C

blocks.hint: The possible types are AA, AB, AC, BB and BC. The physical subsets producing these types do not have equal counts. Given C, choose one of the four remaining physical tiles.
blocks.solution:
1. There are five types: AA, AB, AC, BB and BC. There is no CC type because only one C is available.

  2. \[P(\text{AB})=\frac{\binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{1}}{\binom{5}{2}}=\frac{4}{10}=\frac{2}{5}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{an A}\mid\text{C selected})=\frac{\binom{2}{1}}{\binom{4}{1}}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

    The five visible types cannot be used as an equally likely denominator for this physical-subset experiment.

blocks.html: For an unknown pool size, keep the original counting equation. State the minimum size and integer restrictions, form the count or probability equation, solve it, then substitute every surviving candidate into the original expression. Cancel only factors known to be nonzero. A zero-size selection gives \(\binom{n}{0}=1\) for every nonnegative integer \(n\), so that condition alone cannot determine the pool size.

glossary.definition: An unordered selection of distinct objects; its membership determines the outcome.
The numbers of selected members from each specified category.
Categories with no individual belonging to more than one of them.
A construction represents every intended outcome the same number of times, so one fixed division is valid.
A selected person who is permitted to hold the chair role under the stated rule.
A named person who must be reserved before the remaining places are filled.
A specified nonempty set of named people must be included in full or excluded in full.
Both people from one specified pair belong to the selection.
A disjoint group defined by belonging to the first category only, the second only, both or neither.
The retained number of each letter or object type in an unordered visible selection.
A selection identified by the actual distinct objects, even when some display the same letter or colour.
Only the outcomes satisfying the given condition; its size must be positive to form a count ratio.

examples.title: Count a committee, then distinguish its roles
examples.question: Eight distinct people are available. Count three-person committees, appointments to three different named roles, and three-person committees with one member appointed chair. No person can hold more than one named role.
solution:
There are \(8\cdot7\cdot6=336\) ordered lists of three different people. Each committee occurs in exactly \(3!=6\) orders.

\[N(\text{committee})=\frac{8\cdot7\cdot6}{3!}=\binom{8}{3}=56.\]

Three different named roles distinguish those orders, so their number is \(336\). A committee with only one chair has three choices of chair within each committee:

\[N(\text{committee and chair})=3\binom{8}{3}=168.\]

Choosing the chair first gives the same answer: eight chair choices, followed by two unordered ordinary members from the other seven.

\[8\binom{7}{2}=168.\]

examples.title: Separate composition cases before adding them
examples.question: A pool contains five experienced people and four new people, all distinct. Select four. Count committees with exactly two new members and with at least two new members. Then count committees with exactly two new members and an experienced chair.
solution:
If \(k\) new people are selected, the other \(4-k\) are experienced. The categories are disjoint, so the count for that fixed composition is

\[\binom{4}{k}\binom{5}{4-k}.\]
New members \(k\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)\(4\)
Committee count\(5\)\(40\)\(60\)\(20\)\(1\)

\[N(\text{exactly two new})=\binom{4}{2}\binom{5}{2}=60.\]\[N(\text{at least two new})=60+20+1=81.\]

The cases are disjoint and their full sum is \(126=\binom{9}{4}\).

Every committee with exactly two new people has two experienced people, hence two eligible chairs:

\[N(\text{with experienced chair})=60\cdot2=120.\]

Equivalently, choose the experienced chair first, then one of the remaining four experienced people and two of the four new people:

\[5\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{2}=120.\]

The chair has already occupied one committee place.

examples.title: Reserve named members before filling the remaining places
examples.question: Use the same pool of five experienced and four new people, selecting four. Two new people are named \(N_1\) and \(N_2\). Count committees containing both named people, neither, exactly one, or both-or-neither. Separately, require \(N_1\), exclude \(N_2\), and require exactly two new members; count those committees and all committees satisfying just the two named rules.
solution:
There are seven other people. Both names occupy two places; neither name leaves four places to fill:

\[N(\text{both})=\binom{7}{2}=21,\qquad N(\text{neither})=\binom{7}{4}=35.\]

\[N(\text{exactly one})=2\binom{7}{3}=70.\]\[N(\text{both or neither})=21+35=56.\]

Exactly one, both and neither total \(70+21+35=126\).

For the separate composition restriction, reserve \(N_1\) and remove \(N_2\). One further new person must come from the two remaining new people, and two experienced people from the five available:

\[N=\binom{2}{1}\binom{5}{2}=20.\]

If only the named rules apply, choose the remaining three members from seven people:

\[N(\text{named rules only})=\binom{7}{3}=35.\]

Do not count \(N_1\) again in the remaining new-person quota.

examples.title: Count complete pairs without designating the same pair twice
examples.question: Eight distinct people are arranged into four specified pairs. Select three people. Count selections containing exactly one complete pair, and selections containing no complete pair.
solution:
Choose the complete pair in four ways, then one other person from the remaining six:

\[N(\text{one complete pair})=4\cdot6=24.\]

A three-person selection cannot contain two complete pairs, so this construction is unique.

For no complete pair, choose three of the four pairs, then one person from each selected pair:

\[N(\text{no complete pair})=\binom{4}{3}\cdot2^3=32.\]

\[24+32=56=\binom{8}{3}.\]

If a larger selection can contain several complete pairs, fix the exact number of complete pairs first; merely designating one would count some selections repeatedly.

examples.title: Use disjoint membership regions for overlapping skills
examples.question: Twelve people comprise three music-only people, four sport-only people, two with both skills, and three with neither. Select three distinct people, allowing people from any of the four regions. Count committees in which both skills are represented.
solution: The total is \(\binom{12}{3}=220\). Having both skills represented does not require every member to possess a skill. Start by excluding committees missing a required skill.

Seven people have no music skill: the four sport-only people and the three with neither. Six have no sport skill: the three music-only people and the three with neither.

\[N(\text{no music})=\binom{7}{3}=35,\qquad N(\text{no sport})=\binom{6}{3}=20.\]

The committee containing all three people with neither skill was subtracted twice. Add it back once:

\[N(\text{both skills represented})=\binom{12}{3}-\binom{7}{3}-\binom{6}{3}+\binom{3}{3}=166.\]

A dual-skilled person contributes to both skill requirements but remains one selected person. Multiplying a music-member choice by a sport-member choice can select that same person twice or represent one committee more than once.

examples.title: Count unordered types, then weight physical selections
examples.question: The six physical tiles are A, A, B, B, B and C. Select three tiles without order. Count the possible letter-type selections. Find the probability of type ABC under (i) a uniform choice among those types and (ii) a uniform choice among physical three-tile subsets.
solution:
Let \((a,b,c)\) be the retained numbers of As, Bs and Cs. Require

\[a+b+c=3,\qquad0\le a\le2,\quad0\le b\le3,\quad0\le c\le1,\]

with integer counts. If \(c=0\), the types are BBB, ABB and AAB. If \(c=1\), they are BBC, ABC and AAC. There are six types.

A uniform choice among the six types gives

\[P(\text{ABC})=\frac{1}{6}.\]

For physical subsets, the total is \(\binom{6}{3}=20\). Type ABC can use either A, any of the three Bs and the one C:

\[P(\text{ABC})=\frac{\binom{2}{1}\binom{3}{1}\binom{1}{1}}{\binom{6}{3}}=\frac{6}{20}=\frac{3}{10}.\]
The physical subset counts for BBB, ABB, AAB, BBC, ABC and AAC are respectively \(1,6,3,3,6,1\), which sum to \(20\). They are unequal; the sampling rule matters.

examples.title: Recover an unknown pool size from a selection probability
examples.question: A three-person committee is selected uniformly from \(n\) distinct people, including two named people A and B. The probability that both named people are selected is \(\frac{1}{7}\). Find every possible value of \(n\).
solution:
The pool must contain at least three people, so \(n\) is an integer with \(n\ge3\). If A and B are included, choose the one remaining member from \(n-2\) people:

\[\frac{\binom{n-2}{1}}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{1}{7}.\]

Here \(n-2>0\), so the common factor may be cancelled:

\[\frac{6}{n(n-1)}=\frac{1}{7},\qquad n^2-n-42=0.\]

\[(n-7)(n+6)=0.\]

The algebraic candidates are \(7\) and \(-6\). Only \(7\) is a permissible pool size.

\[\frac{\binom{5}{1}}{\binom{7}{3}}=\frac{5}{35}=\frac{1}{7}.\]

The original probability confirms \(n=7\). A noninteger positive root would also have to be rejected.

extraPractice.title: A committee and its officers are different outcomes
extraPractice.prompt: Eleven distinct people, including X, are available. Count four-person committees with no offices assigned, committees with one member designated chair, and committees with a chair and a different member designated secretary. If one committee-with-chair outcome is chosen uniformly, find the probability that X is chair.
extraPractice.hint: A selected committee has four possible chairs and then three possible secretaries. For X chair, fix X and choose the other three committee members from the remaining ten.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N(\text{committee})=\binom{11}{4}=330.\]
  2. \[N(\text{committee and chair})=330\times4=1320.\]
  3. \[N(\text{two different officers})=330\times4\times3=3960.\]

  4. Fixing X as chair leaves \(\binom{10}{3}=120\) committees:

    \[P(\text{X chairs})=\frac{120}{1320}=\frac{1}{11}.\]

    The roles are labelled, but the ordinary committee members are not placed in an order.

extraPractice.title: Three categories and a restricted chair
extraPractice.prompt: A pool contains \(5\) engineers, \(3\) designers and \(2\) analysts. The categories are disjoint and all ten people are distinct. Select a four-person committee with at least one person from each category. Count the permitted committees, those with more engineers than designers, and committee-with-chair outcomes when the chair must be an analyst. For a uniformly chosen permitted committee with no office assigned, find the probability it has more engineers than designers.

fields.label: Probability of more engineers than designers

extraPractice.hint: The only compositions, in engineer/designer/analyst order, are \((2,1,1),(1,2,1),(1,1,2)\). A committee in the last case has two eligible analyst chairs.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\begin{aligned}N_{211}&=\binom{5}{2}\binom{3}{1}\binom{2}{1}=60,\\N_{121}&=\binom{5}{1}\binom{3}{2}\binom{2}{1}=30,\\N_{112}&=\binom{5}{1}\binom{3}{1}\binom{2}{2}=15.\end{aligned}\]

  2. The permitted total is \(60+30+15=105\). Only composition \((2,1,1)\) has more engineers than designers, giving \(60\).

  3. Assign an analyst chair within each composition:

    \[60(1)+30(1)+15(2)=120.\]

    A single constant chair factor would be wrong because the number of analysts varies.

  4. \[P(\text{more engineers}\mid\text{every category represented})=\frac{60}{105}=\frac{4}{7}.\]

    This last experiment selects an unassigned committee uniformly; its denominator is \(105\), not the number of chair assignments.

extraPractice.title: Read the rule for two named members literally
extraPractice.prompt: A five-person group is selected from eleven distinct people, including A and B. Count groups containing both A and B; groups in which they cannot both serve; and groups in which either both serve or neither serves. Under uniform selection of a five-person group, find the probability that exactly one of A and B is selected given that at least one is selected.

fields.label: A and B cannot both serve
Exactly one given at least one

extraPractice.hint: Partition groups into neither, exactly one and both. “Cannot both” includes the neither case; “both or neither” excludes the exactly-one case.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N(\text{both})=\binom{9}{3}=84,\quad N(\text{neither})=\binom{9}{5}=126,\quad N(\text{exactly one})=2\binom{9}{4}=252.\]

  2. These disjoint counts sum to \(462=\binom{11}{5}\).

    \[N(\text{not both})=126+252=378,\qquad N(\text{both or neither})=84+126=210.\]
  3. \[P(\text{exactly one}\mid\text{at least one})=\frac{252}{252+84}=\frac{3}{4}.\]

extraPractice.title: One person can satisfy two category requirements
extraPractice.prompt: Of ten distinct people, two belong only to music, three only to sport, two to both, and three to neither. Select three people. Count groups with at least one music member and at least one sport member. Also count such groups containing no member of both clubs, and such groups in which every selected person belongs to at least one of the two clubs. Under uniform selection, find the probability that both clubs are represented given that no dual-club member was selected.

fields.label: Both clubs represented, no dual-club member
Both represented; everyone belongs to at least one club
Both represented given no dual-club member

extraPractice.hint: The four stated membership regions are disjoint. Use the complement of missing music or missing sport; the two missing-club events overlap when everyone selected belongs to neither.
extraPractice.solution:
1. There are six people outside music, five outside sport and three outside both. Hence

    \[N(\text{both represented})=\binom{10}{3}-\binom{6}{3}-\binom{5}{3}+\binom{3}{3}=120-20-10+1=91.\]

  2. Excluding the two dual-club members leaves eight people. The outside-music, outside-sport and neither counts remain six, five and three:

    \[N(\text{both represented, no dual member})=\binom{8}{3}-20-10+1=27.\]

  3. Excluding the three people in neither club leaves seven. Missing music then means selecting three sport-only members; missing sport is impossible because only two music-only members exist:

    \[N(\text{both represented, no neither member})=\binom{7}{3}-1=34.\]

  4. The conditioning event is simply no dual-club member; it contains all \(\binom{8}{3}=56\) groups:

    \[P=\frac{27}{56}.\]

    A dual-club member alone would meet both representation requirements, so the music and sport categories must not be treated as disjoint.

extraPractice.title: An inverse probability must give an integer pool size
extraPractice.prompt: Three people are chosen uniformly from \(n\) distinct people, including A and B, where \(n\ge3\) is an integer. The probability that both A and B are selected is \(\frac{3}{28}\). Find \(n\), the probability neither is selected, and the probability A is selected given that at least one of A and B is selected. In a separate model of the same form, could the probability of selecting both be exactly \(\frac{1}{8}\)?

fields.label: A selected given at least one name
Can the separate model have probability \(\frac{1}{8}\)?

options.possible: Yes, for an integer pool size.
options.impossible: No integer pool size gives that probability.

extraPractice.hint: For both names, choose one other person. Divide by the total number of three-person groups. Keep the integer domain when solving the resulting equation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\text{both})=\frac{\binom{n-2}{1}}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{6}{n(n-1)}.\]

    Cancellation is valid because \(n\ge3\).

  2. \[\frac{6}{n(n-1)}=\frac{3}{28}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n(n-1)=56\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(n-8)(n+7)=0.\]

    Only \(n=8\) satisfies the original domain.

  3. \[P(\text{neither})=\frac{\binom{6}{3}}{\binom{8}{3}}=\frac{20}{56}=\frac{5}{14}.\]

  4. The at-least-one conditioning count is \(56-20=36\). Groups containing A number \(\binom{7}{2}=21\), and all satisfy the condition:

    \[P(\text{A}\mid\text{A or B})=\frac{21}{36}=\frac{7}{12}.\]

  5. The separate probability \(\frac{1}{8}\) would require \(n(n-1)=48\). But \(7\cdot6=42<48<56=8\cdot7\), and the product increases for integers \(n\ge3\). No integer size works; rounding a noninteger algebraic root would change the probability.

starters.title: Exactly one complete pair leaves two singles from different pairs
starters.question: Ten distinct people form five specified, disjoint pairs. A four-person group is chosen. Count groups containing exactly one complete pair, exactly two complete pairs, and no complete pair. Under uniform selection of a four-person group, find the probability of exactly one complete pair given that at least one complete pair is selected.
starters.hint: For exactly one pair, choose that pair, then choose two different remaining pairs and one member from each. Taking both singles from the same pair would create a second complete pair.
starters.solution:
1. \[N(\text{exactly one pair})=5\binom{4}{2}2^2=120.\]

    The one complete pair is uniquely identified in each counted group.

  2. \[N(\text{exactly two pairs})=\binom{5}{2}=10.\]

    The two selected complete pairs are unordered; do not label a first pair.

  3. \[N(\text{no complete pair})=\binom{5}{4}2^4=80.\]

    Choose four different source pairs and one of two members from each.

  4. Check the partition: \(120+10+80=210=\binom{10}{4}\).

    \[P(\text{exactly one}\mid\text{at least one})=\frac{120}{120+10}=\frac{12}{13}.\]

starters.title: Unordered letter types need not be equally likely physical samples
starters.question: Seven physical tiles show A, A, A, A, B, B, C. Select three tiles without replacement; their order is ignored. First count the possible visible letter multisets. In experiment I, each three-tile subset of the seven physical tiles is equally likely. In experiment II, each possible visible three-letter multiset is equally likely. Find the probability of one of each letter in each experiment. In experiment I, also find the probability of one of each letter given that C is selected.
starters.hint: List feasible multiplicities \((a,b,c)\) with \(a+b+c=3\), \(a\le4\), \(b\le2\), \(c\le1\). For physical sampling, a letter multiset has weight \(\binom{4}{a}\binom{2}{b}\binom{1}{c}\), not automatically one.
starters.solution:
1. The visible multisets are AAA, AAB, AAC, ABB, ABC and BBC: six possibilities. BBB is unavailable because only two Bs exist; any repeated C is also impossible.

  2. Experiment I has \(\binom{7}{3}=35\) equally likely physical subsets. ABC can be formed by choosing one of four A tiles, one of two B tiles and the one C:

    \[P_{\mathrm{I}}(ABC)=\frac{\binom{4}{1}\binom{2}{1}\binom{1}{1}}{\binom{7}{3}}=\frac{8}{35}.\]

  3. The physical weights for AAA, AAB, AAC, ABB, ABC, BBC are \(4,12,6,4,8,1\), summing to \(35\). They are not equal.

  4. Experiment II explicitly weights the six visible multisets equally. Only ABC has one of each letter, so \(P_{\mathrm{II}}(ABC)=\frac{1}{6}\).

  5. In experiment I, fixing the one C leaves an unordered choice of two physical tiles from the other six:

    \[N(C\text{ selected})=\binom{6}{2}=15,\qquad P_{\mathrm{I}}(ABC\mid C)=\frac{8}{15}.\]

    Use the physical conditional sample space for this question, preserving its original sampling rule.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: respect the available multiplicity of each letter.
  • 1 mark: enumerate the six feasible unordered visible types without duplicate orders.
  • 1 mark: count the physical three-tile subsets.
  • 1 mark: count physical subsets giving ABC.
  • 1 mark: obtain the physical probability.
  • 1 mark: distinguish uniform visible-type selection and obtain its probability.
  • 1 mark: count physical subsets satisfying the C condition.
  • 1 mark: obtain the conditional probability under the original physical model.

revision.body:
Define one complete selection. Count its composition and membership conditions exactly once.

Does order or an assigned role matter?

\[\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}=\frac{{}^{n}P_r}{r!},\qquad\binom{n}{0}=\binom{n}{n}=1.\]

For distinct objects use integers \(0\le r\le n\). A committee has no internal order. If all selected members are eligible, a chair gives \(r\) choices; two distinct officers give \(r(r-1)\). An impossible selection has count zero; never evaluate a negative factorial.

Build disjoint compositions before counting

From disjoint groups of sizes \(a\) and \(b\), an \(r\)-person selection with \(k\) from the first group has

\[N_k=\binom{a}{k}\binom{b}{r-k},\qquad\max(0,r-b)\le k\le\min(a,r).\]

Use integer counts with \(0\le r\le a+b\). Sum feasible cases for at-least or at-most conditions. For overlapping categories, split into disjoint membership regions first. Choosing a designated member before the group can create variable overcounting.

Apply named-member rules before filling places

For two named people among \(n\ge2\), choosing \(r\) people gives:

\[N_{\text{both}}=\binom{n-2}{r-2},\quad N_{\text{neither}}=\binom{n-2}{r},\quad N_{\text{exactly one}}=2\binom{n-2}{r-1}.\]

Treat out-of-range selections as zero. “Not both” includes neither; “both or neither” excludes exactly one. For complete-pair restrictions, choose the source pairs, then their selected members; prevent extra complete pairs when required.

Keep the sampling model and denominator consistent

\[P(E\mid F)=\frac{N(E\cap F)}{N(F)},\qquad N(F)>0.\]

This count ratio requires equally likely elementary outcomes. A visible letter-multiplicity vector counts once, but its physical-subset weight is a product such as \(\binom{a}{i}\binom{b}{j}\). Do not assume the visible types are uniform. Recover unknown sizes within their integer domain and verify the original probability.

revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_count_allocations.description: Count allocations to named or unnamed groups. Decide whether positions or memberships matter and identify the right denominator for probability.

sections.title: Does each group have a name or a job?
sections.label: Labelled assignments
sections.intro:
First say what one outcome records: each person’s destination, membership of unnamed groups, or exact seats. A group is labelled when its name, location or job matters. Swapping the whole membership of team X with team Y changes an assignment even if their sizes agree.

To assign \(n\) distinct people to labelled groups of fixed sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_k\), choose each group from the people still available. With nonnegative integer sizes summing to \(n\),

\[N=\frac{n!}{n_1!n_2!\cdots n_k!}.\]

The factorials remove order inside each group. If \(r\) people remain unassigned, the assigned sizes sum to \(n-r\) and the denominator also includes \(r!\). Their residual set is forced by the assignments; it is not interchangeable with an assigned team of the same size. Use \(0!=1\) for an empty labelled group.

blocks.html: Equal capacity does not erase a name. Two stations, two boxes and two physical rows can remain distinguishable even when they hold the same number of objects. Remove a distinction only when the stated outcome ignores it.

blocks.title: Keep the unassigned people as one residual set
blocks.prompt: From eight distinct people, assign two to team X, one to team Y and three to team Z. The remaining two are unassigned. No person can belong to more than one team. Count the assignments, ignoring order within each team.
blocks.hint: Choose X, then Y from those left, then Z from those still left. The unassigned set is forced. It is not interchangeable with team X merely because both contain two people.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N=\binom{8}{2}\binom{6}{1}\binom{5}{3}=28\cdot6\cdot10=1680.\]

  2. Equivalently,

    \[N=\frac{8!}{2!\,1!\,3!\,2!}=1680.\]

    The last factorial removes the internal order of the unassigned set; it does not remove a team label.

blocks.html:
If capacities are not fixed, count destinations instead. For \(n\) distinct objects, each independently assigned to any of \(k\ge1\) labelled boxes, there are \(k^n\) assignments when empty boxes are allowed. Requiring two named objects to share a box lets you assign them as one destination-unit, then assign the other objects.

For three boxes and \(n\ge1\), exactly one used box gives three assignments. Exactly two used boxes gives \(\binom{3}{2}(2^n-2)\): choose the two boxes, then exclude the two assignments using only one. Therefore all three boxes are used in

\[3^n-3-\binom{3}{2}(2^n-2)=3^n-3\cdot2^n+3\]

assignments. These are destination choices, not fixed-capacity group counts.

sections.title: When may I forget group labels?
sections.label: Unnamed divisions
sections.intro:
An unnamed division records a collection of nonempty groups, without ordering those groups. Count with temporary names, then determine how many name assignments describe each intended division. With no additional restrictions, prescribed positive group sizes give the following count when equal-size groups have no distinguishing roles. Let \(m_s\) be the number of groups of size \(s\):

\[N_{\text{unnamed}}=\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!}\,\frac{1}{\prod_s m_s!}.\]

The product means multiply one repeated-size factorial for each size. Different sizes already distinguish groups. In a restricted problem, first count the valid labelled allocations. Divide that valid count only when the restriction is unchanged by the forgotten label swaps and every intended outcome has the same number of valid labelled versions. Empty labelled boxes require their own destination model; do not treat repeated empty sets as nonempty groups in this division rule.

blocks.html:
Divide seven people into two groups of two and one group of three.

Two different named allocations

GroupAllocation 1Allocation 2
\(X\)\(\{A,B\}\)\(\{C,D\}\)
\(Y\)\(\{C,D\}\)\(\{A,B\}\)
\(Z\)\(\{E,F,G\}\)\(\{E,F,G\}\)

With the names removed, both give \(\bigl\{\{A,B\},\{C,D\},\{E,F,G\}\bigr\}\). Only the two pairs can exchange labels, so there are \(\frac{\binom{7}{2}\binom{5}{2}}{2!}=\frac{210}{2}=105\) unnamed divisions.

The two pairs can exchange temporary names, while the three-person group is identified by its size. Each unnamed division corresponds to exactly two named assignments.

Do not divide by the number of groups factorial automatically. A station-specific rule can distinguish equal-size groups. Also, if you identify a group by its fixed member before counting, the label ambiguity may already have been removed. Check the actual number of representations of each final outcome.

blocks.title: Forget only names that describe the same outcome
blocks.prompt: Eight distinct people are divided into groups of sizes two, two and four. First count assignments to named groups X, Y and Z of those respective sizes. Then count divisions in which all three groups are unnamed and only their memberships matter.
blocks.hint: The two pairs can exchange the temporary names X and Y. The four-person group is already distinguished by its size. Do not divide by three factorial.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{named}}=\binom{8}{2}\binom{6}{2}=420.\]
  2. \[N_{\text{unnamed}}=\frac{420}{2!}=210.\]

    Every unnamed division has exactly two compatible assignments of these temporary names.

blocks.html: The model uses a separate smaller pool of six people divided into three pairs. Compare named assignments with unnamed divisions, then impose a condition that does not depend on the group names.

sections.title: Am I choosing row members or fixing seats?
sections.label: Rows and empty positions
sections.intro:
Distinct fixed seats create a new outcome whenever two people exchange positions. For fully occupied rows of sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_k\), choosing row memberships and then ordering each row gives

\[\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!}\,n_1!\cdots n_k!=n!.\]

Equal-length rows are still different physical locations. Adjacency is within a row and stops at its boundary. To count two named people in the same row, add the permitted ordered seat pairs within each row. For adjacency, count only neighboring seat pairs, in both orders.

blocks.html:
With eight people in two distinct rows of four seats, choose their shared row, its two other occupants, then both row orders. \(N(\text{same row})=2\binom{6}{2}(4!)^2=17280\).

For adjacency, choose their row, one of its three neighbouring seat pairs and the order of the two people. \(N(\text{adjacent})=2\times3\times2!\times6!=8640\).

\(P(\text{adjacent}\mid\text{same row})=\frac{8640}{17280}=\frac12\).

Two rows of four seats contain six neighboring seat pairs. The row break creates no extra adjacency. Same-row membership allows more seat pairs than adjacency does.

If \(r\) distinct people occupy \(r\) of \(m\) fixed seats, with \(0\le r\le m\), choose the occupied positions and order the people:

\[\binom{m}{r}r!=\frac{m!}{(m-r)!}.\]

The \(m-r\) empty positions are not differently named objects. For a single straight row, blocks and gaps can impose patterns of vacancies. A compact list of people with no specified empty positions is a different model; do not add vacant-seat choices unless seats exist in the question.

blocks.title: A vacant seat still has a fixed position
blocks.prompt: Five distinct people, including K and L, occupy five of six fixed seats arranged in two distinct rows of three. One seat remains empty. Count all seatings. Then count those with K in the front row and L in the back row.
blocks.hint: Choose distinct seats for the five people. For the restricted count, place K and L first, then seat the other three people in three of the four remaining seats.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N=\binom{6}{5}5!=\frac{6!}{1!}=720.\]
  2. \[N(\text{K front, L back})=3\cdot3\cdot\frac{4!}{1!}=216.\]

    The unoccupied seat may be in either row. No extra factor labels that empty place.

sections.title: How do named people and category blocks restrict a division?
sections.label: Restricted groups and rows
sections.intro:
Place required members or roles first, reduce the remaining capacities, then allocate the other people. For a same-group condition, split by every possible group when their capacities or roles differ. For a different-group condition, count the permitted group choices or subtract the same-group cases from the total.

A group can be uniquely identified by one of its members. When each team contains one specified mentor, anchoring the team containing mentor M already picks out that team. Do not divide an anchored construction by a group-swap factor again.

blocks.title: Let the mentors identify the teams
blocks.prompt: Two distinct mentors M and N and four distinct trainees form two teams of three, each containing one mentor. Count assignments to named stations East and West. Then count the teams when the group containing M and the group containing N are recorded only by their members, without station assignments.
blocks.hint: For named stations, first assign the two mentors. For membership-only teams, anchor the team containing M and choose its two trainees; the other team is forced.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{stations}}=2!\binom{4}{2}=12.\]
  2. \[N_{\text{membership only}}=\binom{4}{2}=6.\]

    Each membership-only outcome already has one uniquely identified M-team. Dividing this anchored count by two again would lose valid outcomes.

blocks.html: For category blocks in several rows, first decide which complete blocks fit each row’s capacity. Then order those blocks within that row and order the distinct people inside each block. A block cannot cross a physical row boundary. If no collection of complete blocks fills the required capacities, that case contributes zero.

sections.title: Which count belongs in the conditional denominator?
sections.label: Uniform and conditional counts
sections.intro:
A count ratio gives a probability only for equally likely elementary outcomes. State whether the random experiment is uniform over named allocations, unnamed divisions or fixed-seat arrangements. For fixed group sizes, forgetting names gives uniform unnamed divisions only when each division has the same number of named versions. Similarly, full seatings give uniform row-membership assignments when each assignment has the same number of within-row orders.

\[P(E\mid F)=\frac{N(E\cap F)}{N(F)},\qquad N(F)>0.\]

Use the same outcome model in both counts. For the earlier eight-person seating, adjacency J implies the same-row event S, so \(P(J\mid S)=\frac{8640}{17280}=\frac{1}{2}\). The probability of J without that condition instead uses all \(40320\) seatings.

blocks.html: Name the condition before calculating. Count all outcomes satisfying it for the denominator, then add every disjoint case also satisfying the requested event. Keep actual row locations and adjacency boundaries visible in the working.

blocks.title: Condition on the correct row event
blocks.prompt: Seven distinct people are seated uniformly in seven fixed seats: one row of three and one row of four. Let S mean that A and B sit in the same row, and J mean that they occupy adjacent seats within a row. Find the counts for S and J, and the probability of J given S.

fields.label: Seatings with A and B in the same row
Seatings with A and B adjacent
Probability of adjacency given the same row

blocks.hint: For S, count ordered choices of two seats within each row. For J, the two rows have two and three adjacent seat pairs. Arrange the other five people in the remaining seats.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N(S)=(3\cdot2+4\cdot3)5!=18\cdot120=2160.\]
  2. \[N(J)=2[(3-1)+(4-1)]5!=10\cdot120=1200.\]

    The factor two places A and B in either order within each adjacent pair.

  3. Every J seating is also an S seating, so

    \[P(J\mid S)=\frac{1200}{2160}=\frac{5}{9}.\]

    The denominator is the same-row count, not all \(7!\) seatings.

glossary.definition: A group distinguished by its name, location, task or another stated role.
An assignment of each selected person or object to a specified destination.
The prescribed number of people or objects assigned to a group or row.
The unassigned people left after the required groups have been chosen; their role differs from an assigned team.
A collection of nonempty member groups without names or an ordering of the groups.
The number of temporary named assignments that represent one intended unnamed outcome.
A group identified by a specified member or role before its remaining members are chosen.
A distinct physical position, so exchanging its occupant changes the seating.
Only some of the fixed available seats are occupied.
The break between physical rows; adjacency does not continue across it.
A consecutive group of vacant positions that is not adjacent to another vacant position.
A count restricted to all outcomes satisfying the stated condition, with the requested event imposed as an additional restriction.

examples.title: Fill labelled groups from the people still available
examples.question: Seven distinct people must form team X of size two, team Y of size two and team Z of size three. The team names matter, but there is no order within a team. Count the assignments.
solution:
Choose the two people in X. From the remaining five, choose the two in Y. The remaining three form Z:

\[N=\binom{7}{2}\binom{5}{2}\binom{3}{3}=21\cdot10\cdot1=210.\]

The equivalent factorial expression is

\[N=\frac{7!}{2!\,2!\,3!}=210.\]

Its denominator removes order inside each team. Swapping the entire memberships of X and Y still creates a different named assignment.

examples.title: Remove only the repeated equal-size group labels
examples.question: Divide seven distinct people into two unnamed pairs and one unnamed three-person group. Count the divisions. In a separate problem, divide six distinct people into three unnamed pairs.
solution:
Temporarily name the two pairs X and Y and the triple Z. There are \(210\) named assignments. Each unnamed division produces two such assignments by swapping X and Y; its triple is distinguished by size.

\[N=\frac{7!}{2!\,2!\,3!\,2!}=105.\]

For six people in three pairs, the temporary named-group count is

\[\frac{6!}{(2!)^3}=90.\]

Each unnamed division has \(3!=6\) assignments of the three temporary names, giving

\[N=\frac{6!}{(2!)^3\,3!}=15.\]
The first problem uses a factor \(2!\), not \(3!\). Only groups of the same size and with no distinguishing role can exchange their temporary names without changing the intended outcome.

examples.title: Separate same-row membership from adjacency
examples.question: Eight distinct people fill two distinct rows of four fixed seats. Count all seatings, those with A and B in the same row, and those with A and B adjacent within one row.
solution:
All eight seats are distinct, so there are \(8!=40320\) seatings. Equivalently, choose the front-row members, then order both rows:

\[\binom{8}{4}4!4!=40320.\]

For the same row, choose their row, choose two seats in that row, order A and B, then seat everyone else:

\[N(S)=2\binom{4}{2}2!6!=17280.\]

Each row has three adjacent seat pairs. Choose the row and pair, order A and B, then fill the remaining six seats:

\[N(J)=2\cdot3\cdot2!\cdot6!=8640.\]
The last seat of one row and first seat of another are not adjacent. Treating the room as one eight-seat line would incorrectly create a seventh adjacent pair instead of the actual six.

examples.title: Count vacancies without giving them artificial identities
examples.question: Five distinct people occupy five of nine fixed positions in one straight row; the four remaining positions are empty. Count all seatings, those with all four empty positions consecutive, those with no adjacent empty positions, and those with exactly one adjacent empty pair while the other two empty positions are isolated from that pair and from each other.
solution:
Choose the occupied positions and order the five people:

\[N=\binom{9}{5}5!=\frac{9!}{4!}=15120.\]

The four vacancies are identical as symbols; the physical positions are still distinct.

If the four empty positions form one block, arrange that block with the five distinct people:

\[N(\text{one empty block})=6!=720.\]

Arrange the five people first in \(5!=120\) orders. Their row has six gaps including both ends. For four isolated empty positions, choose four different gaps:

\[N(\text{isolated empties})=5!\binom{6}{4}=1800.\]

For exactly one adjacent empty pair, choose its gap, then two different remaining gaps for the two isolated empties:

\[N(\text{one pair and two singles})=5!\cdot6\binom{5}{2}=7200.\]

The pair is a maximal empty run of length two. Using the same gap for an extra vacancy would create a longer run; choosing two pair gaps would produce two adjacent pairs instead.

examples.title: Assign mentors before allocating the other members
examples.question: Three distinct mentors and four distinct trainees form teams for named stations X, Y and Z. X needs three people; Y and Z need two each. Every station must have exactly one mentor. Count the assignments. Then count them if a specified mentor is fixed at each specified station.
solution: Assign the three mentors to the three named stations in \(3!=6\) ways.

X still needs two trainees. Y and Z each need one:

\[N_{\text{trainees}}=\binom{4}{2}\binom{2}{1}=6\cdot2=12.\]

\[N=3!\binom{4}{2}\binom{2}{1}=72.\]

Y and Z have equal capacities, but their station names still matter.
When every mentor’s station is specified, the mentor-assignment factor becomes one. The count is therefore \(12\), without another division by \(3!\).

examples.title: Keep every category block inside one physical row
examples.question: Eight distinct people belong to three disjoint categories: three painters, three musicians and two technicians. They fill one row of three fixed seats and a second row of five fixed seats. All members of each category must occupy consecutive seats within a single row. Count the seatings.
solution: The row of three must contain all three painters or all three musicians. It cannot contain just the two technicians, and it cannot take part of another category without splitting that category. There are two category choices for the short row.

Order the short row in \(3!\) ways. In the long row, the remaining triple and the technician pair form two distinguishable blocks. Choose their order, then order the people inside both blocks:

\[N=2\cdot3!\cdot2!\cdot3!\cdot2!=288.\]
A block must not cross the break between the rows. Counting arbitrary orders of three blocks in one continuous eight-seat line would include invalid seatings.

examples.title: Separate the cases for four named people before conditioning
examples.question: Eight distinct people, including A, B, C and D, fill two distinct rows of four fixed seats uniformly. Let S mean that A and B are in the same row. Find the probability that C and D are also in the same row, given S.
solution:
Choose A and B’s common row, choose and order their seats, then arrange the other six people:

\[N(S)=2\binom{4}{2}2!6!=17280.\]

In the desired event, the two named pairs may share a row or occupy opposite rows. These cases are disjoint.

If all four named people are in one row, choose that row and order both rows:

\[N_1=2\cdot4!\cdot4!=1152.\]

If the two pairs occupy opposite rows, choose A and B’s row. Choose which two of the four other people join them; the remaining two join C and D. Then order both rows:

\[N_2=2\binom{4}{2}4!4!=6912.\]

\[P(\text{C and D same row}\mid S)=\frac{1152+6912}{17280}=\frac{8064}{17280}=\frac{7}{15}.\]

Ignoring the all-four-in-one-row case would omit valid outcomes.
