extraPractice.title: Only the two equal groups lose their names
extraPractice.prompt: Ten distinct people, including A and B, form groups of sizes \(3,3,4\), with no order inside a group. First count allocations to named groups Red, Blue and Green of those respective sizes. Then count divisions with no group names, and unnamed divisions in which A and B are together. Under a uniform choice of an unnamed division, find the probability that B is with A given that A is in the four-person group.

fields.label: Allocations to the three named groups
Unnamed divisions with A and B together
B with A given A is in the four-person group

extraPractice.hint: Only the two triples can exchange unnamed labels. For A and B together, separate the cases where their group has size four or three.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{named}}=\binom{10}{4}\binom{6}{3}=4200,\qquad N_{\text{unnamed}}=\frac{4200}{2!}=2100.\]

    The four-person group is distinguished by its size.

  2. If A and B are in the four-person group, choose its two other members, then divide the remaining six into two unnamed triples:

    \[N_4=\binom{8}{2}\frac{\binom{6}{3}}{2!}=280.\]

  3. If A and B are in a triple, choose its third member, then the other triple. The triple containing A and B is already identified, so it is not divided away:

    \[N_3=8\binom{7}{3}=280.\]

    Thus \(N(\text{together})=280+280=560\).

  4. Given that A is in the four-person group, its other members are three of the remaining nine. The full conditioning count is \(\binom{9}{3}\frac{\binom{6}{3}}{2!}=840\).

    \[P(\text{B with A}\mid\text{A in the four-person group})=\frac{280}{840}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

extraPractice.title: Named mentors can identify otherwise unnamed teams
extraPractice.prompt: Three distinct mentors M, N and O and six distinct trainees form three teams of three, each with one mentor. Count assignments to named stations East, West and North. Then remove the station names and count unnamed teams satisfying the same rule. Among the unnamed divisions, count those in which trainee A is with M and trainee B is with N. Under uniform selection of a valid unnamed division, find the probability B is with N given that A is with M.

fields.label: Assignments to the three named stations
A with M and B with N
B with N given A with M

extraPractice.hint: For unnamed teams, use the mentors to identify them and choose each mentor’s two trainees. For the conditional question, the five other trainees occupy one remaining place with M, two with N and two with O.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Assign the mentors to the stations, then choose trainee pairs:

    \[N_{\text{stations}}=3!\binom{6}{2}\binom{4}{2}=540.\]

  2. For unnamed teams, the team containing M, N or O is uniquely identified by that mentor:

    \[N_{\text{teams}}=\binom{6}{2}\binom{4}{2}=90.\]

    Equivalently, \(540\) named assignments have multiplicity \(3!\) per unnamed division.

  3. Fix A with M and B with N. Choose M’s other trainee from the four trainees other than A and B; then choose N’s other trainee from the remaining three. O gets the final pair:

    \[N(\text{A with M, B with N})=4\cdot3=12.\]

  4. If only A is fixed with M, choose M’s partner in five ways and N’s two trainees from the four remaining:

    \[N(\text{A with M})=5\binom{4}{2}=30,\qquad P=\frac{12}{30}=\frac{2}{5}.\]

extraPractice.title: Unequal row lengths change the conditional fraction
extraPractice.prompt: Nine distinct people fill three labelled rows containing respectively two, three and four numbered seats. Adjacency means consecutive positions within the same row; it never crosses between rows. Count all seating arrangements, those with A and B in the same row, and those with A and B adjacent. For a uniformly chosen seating, find the probability of adjacency given that A and B share a row.

fields.label: A and B in the same row

extraPractice.hint: For a row of length \(s\), A and B have \(s(s-1)\) ordered seat choices but only \(2(s-1)\) adjacent ordered choices. Arrange the other seven people afterwards.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{all}}=9!=362880.\]
  2. \[N(S)=\bigl(2\cdot1+3\cdot2+4\cdot3\bigr)7!=20(5040)=100800.\]

    The three row cases are disjoint.

  3. \[N(J)=2\bigl((2-1)+(3-1)+(4-1)\bigr)7!=12(5040)=60480.\]

    Each consecutive seat pair permits AB or BA. A row’s final seat is not adjacent to the next row’s first seat.

  4. Since every adjacent pair shares a row, \(J\subseteq S\):

    \[P(J\mid S)=\frac{60480}{100800}=\frac{3}{5}.\]

    The row lengths are unequal, so do not average three row-specific probabilities without their correct weights.

extraPractice.title: Three empty places have three run patterns
extraPractice.prompt: Five distinct people occupy five of eight numbered seats in a single line. The three empty seats are indistinguishable. Count arrangements in which all empty seats form one consecutive block; in which no two empty seats are adjacent; and in which there is exactly one run of two empty seats and one separate empty seat. Under uniform selection of a seating arrangement, find the probability that no empties are adjacent given that they do not all form one block.

fields.label: All three empties form one block
Exactly one empty pair and one separate empty
No adjacency given not all in one block

extraPractice.hint: Arrange the five people first, creating six gaps including the two ends. Separate empty runs occupy different gaps. The run of two and the single empty have different sizes.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{all}}=\frac{8!}{3!}=6720.\]

    Do not give the three empty seats separate identities.

  2. One block of three empties acts as one object alongside the five distinct people:

    \[N_{\text{block}}=6!=720.\]

  3. For isolated empties, select three of the six gaps:

    \[N_{\text{separated}}=5!\binom{6}{3}=2400.\]

  4. For one run of two and one single, choose two different gaps and assign the two different run lengths:

    \[N_{\text{pair}}=5!\binom{6}{2}2!=3600.\]

    The three cases check the total: \(720+2400+3600=6720\).

  5. \[P(\text{no adjacent empties}\mid\text{not all in one block})=\frac{2400}{6720-720}=\frac{2}{5}.\]

    “Not all together” still allows a run of two; it does not mean complete separation.

extraPractice.title: Free destinations differ from fixed group sizes
extraPractice.prompt: Five distinct parcels, including A and B, are independently assigned to one of three labelled boxes, each box having probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) for each parcel. There are no capacity limits and boxes may be empty. Count all assignments, assignments using exactly two boxes, and assignments using all three boxes. Find the probability that A and B are in the same box given that all three boxes are used.

fields.label: A and B together given all boxes used

extraPractice.hint: Every parcel has three choices. For exactly two used boxes, first choose the pair of boxes and remove the two assignments that put every parcel in just one of them. For A and B together, regard their common destination as one choice.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{all}}=3^5=243.\]

    Every assignment has probability \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^5\), so count ratios are valid.

  2. \[N_{\text{exactly two}}=\binom{3}{2}(2^5-2)=90.\]

    Each assignment using exactly two boxes identifies its used pair uniquely.

  3. Exactly one used box gives three assignments. Therefore

    \[N_{\text{all three}}=243-90-3=150.\]

  4. For A and B together, merge only their destination choice. The resulting four units must use all three boxes. Their valid count is

    \[3^4-\binom{3}{2}(2^4-2)-3=81-42-3=36.\]

    No internal ordering is being counted in a box.

    \[P=\frac{36}{150}=\frac{6}{25}.\]

extraPractice.title: Read the group labels
extraPractice.prompt: Split six different people into two groups of three. Give the number when the groups are named and when they are unnamed.
extraPractice.hint: Choose the first triple. With unnamed groups, each division has been counted twice.
extraPractice.solution:
Choose the first triple. With unnamed groups, each division has been counted twice.

  • Named groups: \(20\)
  • Unnamed groups: \(10\)

extraPractice.title: Only equal groups can swap
extraPractice.prompt: Divide eight different pupils into unnamed groups of sizes three, three and two. How many divisions are possible?
extraPractice.hint: Choose the pair, then choose one of the two triples. Exchanging those triples leaves the same division.
extraPractice.solution:
Choose the pair, then choose one of the two triples. Exchanging those triples leaves the same division.

  • Answer: \(280\)

extraPractice.title: Share a row
extraPractice.prompt: Seat five different pupils on six labelled seats in two rows of three. How many seatings put A and B in the same row?
extraPractice.hint: Select one of the two rows and an ordered pair of its three seats. Then seat the other three in three of the four remaining seats.
extraPractice.solution:
Select one of the two rows and an ordered pair of its three seats. Then seat the other three in three of the four remaining seats.

  • Answer: \(288\)

extraPractice.title: Seats may be empty
extraPractice.prompt: Four different pupils sit in six labelled seats. How many seatings are possible?
extraPractice.hint: Assign one of the unused seats to each pupil in order. The empty seats carry no extra labels.
extraPractice.solution:
Assign one of the unused seats to each pupil in order. The empty seats carry no extra labels.

  • Answer: \(360\)

starters.title: Three named people identify the team cases
starters.question: Nine distinct people, including A, B and C, are divided uniformly into three unnamed teams of three. Count all divisions, those in which A, B and C occupy three different teams, and those in which exactly two of A, B and C are together while the third is in another team. Find the probability that A and B are together given that A and C are in different teams.
starters.hint: For three separate teams, their named members identify them. For exactly two names together, choose that pair, select its unnamed teammate, then split the six remaining people into two unnamed triples.
starters.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{all}}=\frac{\binom{9}{3}\binom{6}{3}}{3!}=280.\]

  2. For separate teams, choose A’s two teammates from the six other people, then B’s two from the remaining four. C receives the remaining pair:

    \[N_{\text{separate}}=\binom{6}{2}\binom{4}{2}=90.\]

  3. Choose which two named people share a team in three ways. Their third member is one of the six unnamed people. The remaining six divide into two unnamed triples:

    \[N_{\text{exactly two}}=3\cdot6\cdot\frac{\binom{6}{3}}{2!}=180.\]

  4. If all three names are together, the other six form two unnamed triples in \(10\) ways. Thus \(90+180+10=280\).

  5. For A with B but separate from C, the count is \(6\cdot10=60\). A and C are together in \(7\cdot10=70\) divisions, because their teammate may be any of the other seven people.

    \[P(\text{A with B}\mid\text{A separate from C})=\frac{60}{280-70}=\frac{2}{7}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: remove the constant multiplicity of the three unnamed team labels.
  • 1 mark: obtain the total of 280 divisions.
  • 1 mark: anchor the three separate teams by A, B and C.
  • 1 mark: obtain 90 separate-team divisions.
  • 1 mark: select the unique pair of named people and count the exactly-two case.
  • 1 mark: identify the conditional numerator as 60.
  • 1 mark: form the denominator by excluding all A-and-C-together divisions.
  • 1 mark: obtain the conditional probability.

starters.title: Two pairs may occupy one row or different rows
starters.question: Eight distinct people fill two labelled rows of four numbered seats, uniformly over all \(8!\) arrangements. A, B, C and D are four different people. Let \(S\) mean that A and B share a row and C and D share a row; the two pairs may be in the same row or different rows. Let \(J\) mean that A and B are adjacent and C and D are adjacent within their rows. Count \(S\) and \(J\). Find the probability that C and D share a row given that A and B share a row, and find \(P(J\mid S)\).
starters.hint: Split both counts into two disjoint cases: all four named people occupy one row, or the named pairs occupy different rows. For adjacency within a full four-seat row, treat AB and CD as two distinct blocks, with two internal orders each.
starters.solution:
1. If both pairs occupy the same row, choose that row and arrange its four named people and the other row’s four people:

    \[N(S_{\text{one row}})=2\cdot4!\cdot4!=1152.\]

  2. If the pairs occupy different rows, choose the row for A and B, choose their two ordered seats, choose the two ordered seats for C and D in the other row, then arrange the remaining people:

    \[N(S_{\text{different rows}})=2(4\cdot3)^2 4!=6912.\]

    Hence \(N(S)=1152+6912=8064\).

  3. For both adjacent pairs in one row, arrange the two blocks and their internal orders:

    \[N(J_{\text{one row}})=2\cdot2!\cdot2^2\cdot4!=384.\]

  4. For adjacent pairs in different rows, each row has three consecutive seat pairs and two orders within the selected pair:

    \[N(J_{\text{different rows}})=2(3\cdot2)^2 4!=1728.\]

    Hence \(N(J)=384+1728=2112\). Adjacency does not cross a row boundary.

  5. A and B share a row in \(2(4\cdot3)6!=17280\) arrangements. Thus

    \[P(\text{C,D same row}\mid\text{A,B same row})=\frac{8064}{17280}=\frac{7}{15}.\]

  6. Every arrangement in \(J\) also satisfies \(S\), so

    \[P(J\mid S)=\frac{2112}{8064}=\frac{11}{42}.\]

    The two conditional questions have different denominators because their given events differ.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: split the same-row event into both-pairs-in-one-row and pairs-in-different-rows cases.
  • 1 mark: count 1152 in the first case.
  • 1 mark: count 6912 in the second case and obtain the same-row total.
  • 1 mark: identify the two adjacency blocks and their internal orders.
  • 1 mark: count the one-row adjacency case.
  • 1 mark: count different-row adjacency using valid consecutive pairs and obtain 2112.
  • 1 mark: count the A-and-B-same-row conditioning event.
  • 1 mark: obtain the first conditional probability.
  • 1 mark: use S as the second denominator and obtain the final conditional probability.

revision.body:
Decide what distinguishes the groups, the people and the positions before choosing a formula.

Are the destinations named, with fixed sizes?

\[N_{\text{labelled}}=\frac{n!}{s_1!s_2!\cdots s_k!},\qquad s_1+\cdots+s_k=n.\]

Use nonnegative integer sizes and distinct people; there is no order inside each group. Treat unassigned people as a separate, identifiable group. With free assignments to \(k\) labelled boxes, empty boxes allowed and no capacity limit, each of \(n\) people has \(k\) choices: \(k^n\), for \(k\ge1\).

Which unnamed groups really can exchange labels?

Divide only by a constant label multiplicity among equivalent nonempty groups. For unnamed sizes \(a,a,b\), where \(a,b\ge1\) and \(a\ne b\):

\[N=\frac{(2a+b)!}{a!a!b!\,2!}.\]

The different size identifies the third group. A required member can identify a team instead. Check that restrictions preserve the label symmetry; named destinations are never swapped away.

Numbered seats require positions as well as membership

\[N=\frac{q!}{(q-n)!},\qquad0\le n\le q.\]

Place \(n\) distinct people in \(q\) distinct seats; empty places have no identities. Restore internal row orders after choosing membership. Adjacency stays within a row. Arrange \(m\) people first to create \(m+1\) gaps, including both ends; isolated empties use different gaps. A block of empties has one internal arrangement.

Keep restrictions and probability outcomes consistent

\[P(E\mid F)=\frac{N(E\cap F)}{N(F)},\qquad N(F)>0.\]

Use equally likely outcomes of the same kind in both counts. Split cases before counting: same row is weaker than adjacency; not all together is weaker than complete separation. For multiple named pairs, distinguish pairs in one row from pairs in different rows.
revision.checks: • Group labels, capacities, internal order, named restrictions, empty-seat identity and conditional denominator?
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_count_mixed_counting.description: Define a finished outcome, track construction multiplicity, and combine roles, restrictions and probability through complete cases.

sections.title: What does one finished outcome record?
sections.label: Construction ledger
sections.intro:
A mixed counting question is a sequence of decisions. Before choosing a formula, write one sentence defining a finished outcome: a set of members, members with named jobs, a string of visible letters, or an assignment to fixed positions. Two constructions give the same outcome exactly when every detail the question records is the same.

For each construction stage, record the choices still available and any restriction that changes them. Multiplication counts complete construction routes when every stage has the stated number of choices for each permitted earlier route. If that number changes, split into cases or add the branch counts.

blocks.html:
Count routes, then check their multiplicity. A product can count a finished object more than once. If every object has exactly \(m\) construction routes, with \(m\ge1\), then

\[N_{\text{objects}}=\frac{N_{\text{routes}}}{m}.\]

Demonstrate the same multiplicity for every object before dividing.

blocks.title: Keep or forget the marked member?
blocks.prompt: Choose four people from nine. First a temporary organiser is chosen, then three other members. Find the number of construction routes, the number of final committees when the organiser is forgotten, and the number of outcomes if the organiser is a real recorded role.
blocks.hint: There are nine initial organiser choices. How many different members of one finished four-person committee could have been chosen first?
blocks.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{routes}}=9\binom{8}{3}=504.\]

  2. Every four-person committee has four possible marked organisers:

    \[N_{\text{committees}}=\frac{504}{4}=126=\binom{9}{4}.\]

  3. When the organiser is a real part of the outcome, its identity must be retained. The count remains \(504\).

blocks.html: When a temporary label can be attached only to eligible members, its multiplicity may depend on the final committee. Removing an actual role and adding a role are opposite operations, but neither is always multiplication or division by the committee size.

Select three people from five seniors and three juniors, with at least one senior.

Effect of recording a senior chair

SeniorsCommitteesChair optionsOutcomes with chair
\(1\)\(\binom{5}{1}\binom{3}{2}=15\)\(1\)\(15\)
\(2\)\(\binom{5}{2}\binom{3}{1}=30\)\(2\)\(60\)
\(3\)\(\binom{5}{3}\binom{3}{0}=10\)\(3\)\(30\)

Without a recorded chair there are \(15+30+10=55\) committees. With a recorded chair there are \(15+60+30=105\) outcomes.

A senior chair can be chosen in one, two or three ways inside different committees. Keep the composition cases visible before forgetting or recording the role.

A successful first step does not make every final committee equally represented. Choosing a senior first counts committees with two seniors twice and committees with three seniors three times. An arbitrary factorial or committee-size divisor cannot repair varying multiplicity.

sections.title: Which selected members can fill each role?
sections.label: Role restrictions
sections.intro:
Separate membership from role assignment. If a selected team has \(j\) members eligible for one recorded job, that team contributes \(j\) outcomes. Two different eligible members filling two different jobs contribute \(j(j-1)\). A role name distinguishes its holder: exchanging a captain and deputy normally changes the outcome.

If eligibility depends on categories, count each possible composition before assigning the jobs. For \(s\) seniors, \(t\) juniors and a team of size \(r\), a case with \(j\) seniors has

\[\binom{s}{j}\binom{t}{r-j}\]

memberships, where \(\max(0,r-t)\le j\le\min(s,r)\) and all quantities are integers. A senior captain requires \(j\ge1\); two distinct senior officers require \(j\ge2\).

blocks.title: Do not apply one role multiplier to every composition
blocks.prompt: Three seniors and four juniors form a three-person team with a senior captain and a different senior deputy. Count the outcomes with exactly two senior team members, those with exactly three senior team members, and the total.
blocks.hint: The two different roles require at least two seniors. For a team with \(j\) seniors, the ordered role count is \(j(j-1)\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[N_2=\binom{3}{2}\binom{4}{1}(2)(1)=24.\]
  2. \[N_3=\binom{3}{3}\binom{4}{0}(3)(2)=6.\]
  3. \[N=24+6=30.\]

    Alternatively choose the ordered senior roles first, then the third member: \(3\cdot2\cdot5=30\).

blocks.html: Try a second complete construction. Assigning required roles first can avoid a long case sum. Check that every finished outcome determines one unique choice of roles and one remaining member set; otherwise the new construction may introduce its own overcount.

Named exclusions must be tested at the correct level. “A and B cannot both belong to the team” removes memberships. “A cannot be deputy” removes role assignments, while A may still be a member. A particular member fixed in a job is already chosen and must be removed from the pool for later distinct roles.

sections.title: Are the cases disjoint, and have all overlaps been handled?
sections.label: Cases and overlaps
sections.intro:
Add cases only when each valid outcome belongs to exactly one case, or explicitly correct their overlaps. Categories such as the number of seniors or the final digit often provide a clean partition. Conditions such as “AB adjacent” and “CD adjacent” can both be true in the same arrangement.

\[N(E\cup F)=N(E)+N(F)-N(E\cap F).\]\[N(\text{exactly one of }E,F)=N(E)+N(F)-2N(E\cap F).\]

The first formula retains the overlap once; the second excludes it completely.

blocks.title: Exactly one and at least one have different counts
blocks.prompt: Six distinct people A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a line. Let E mean A and B are adjacent, and let F mean C and D are adjacent. Each pair may appear in either order. Count arrangements satisfying both events, at least one event, and exactly one event.

fields.label: At least one named pair adjacent

blocks.hint: One adjacent pair acts as one block. For both events, make two blocks and retain both internal orders. Use the overlap differently for “at least one” and “exactly one”.

blocks.html: “At least one” includes the overlap. “Exactly one” excludes it. Likewise, “not both” allows either single event and neither event. Translate the wording into cases before applying a block or gap formula.

Different restrictions can also change the size of later choice pools. For digit numbers, selecting a final zero removes the leading-zero issue automatically; a different last digit leaves zero in the remaining pool. For physical rows of seats, an adjacent block must stay inside one row. Case boundaries should follow the point where the construction rule actually changes.

blocks.title: A final zero changes the first-position choices
blocks.prompt: Using the digits \(0,1,2,3,4\) without repetition, count three-digit numbers divisible by five. Then count those that also contain the digit one.
blocks.hint: The last digit must be zero. The first two positions are different nonzero digits. To include one, choose its position and the other nonzero digit.
blocks.solution:
1. Only zero can be the final digit:

    \[N=4\cdot3=12.\]

  2. Place one in either of the first two positions, then choose the other digit from two, three and four:

    \[N_{\text{contains one}}=2\cdot3=6.\]

    The two cases are disjoint because digits cannot repeat.

blocks.html: Use a small independent check. Check that case counts add to the unrestricted total when they are exhaustive. For a positive event, verify that its count does not exceed the full count. Test a small version by listing actual outcomes before trusting a complicated product.

sections.title: Which outcomes are equally likely in the stated experiment?
sections.label: Probability spaces
sections.intro:
Counting and probability use the same model only when the elementary outcomes being counted are equally likely. A random arrangement of distinct people, a uniform subset of physical tiles, and a uniform selection among different visible strings are different experiments.

\[P(E)=\frac{N(E)}{N(\Omega)},\qquad P(E\mid F)=\frac{N(E\cap F)}{N(F)},\quad N(F)>0.\]

Both numerator and denominator must count outcomes of the same kind. The condition \(F\) becomes the new sample space; impose \(E\) as an additional restriction inside it.

blocks.html:
Choose an unordered physical pair uniformly from \(A_1,A_2,B,C\). Each physical pair has probability \(\frac{1}{6}\).

Visible types and the physical pairs that produce them

Visible typePhysical pairsCount
\(\mathrm{AA}\)\(\{A_1,A_2\}\)\(1\)
\(\mathrm{AB}\)\(\{A_1,B\},\ \{A_2,B\}\)\(2\)
\(\mathrm{AC}\)\(\{A_1,C\},\ \{A_2,C\}\)\(2\)
\(\mathrm{BC}\)\(\{B,C\}\)\(1\)

Given at least one A, there are five eligible pairs, so \(P(\mathrm{AA}\mid\text{at least one A})=\frac{1}{5}\).

Each physical tile pair has the same probability. Visible letter types inherit the number of physical pairs producing them. Conditioning removes the BC pair, leaving five equally likely physical pairs.

blocks.title: Condition on physical pairs with their correct weights
blocks.prompt: A bag holds three red tiles and two blue tiles; the five physical tiles are distinct. Two tiles are selected uniformly from all unordered physical pairs. Count the red-red, red-blue and blue-blue pairs. Given that the selected tiles have the same colour, find the probability that they are red.
blocks.hint: Choose physical objects, then group the pairs by colour. The same-colour condition keeps both red-red and blue-blue pairs.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N(\text{RR})=\binom{3}{2}=3,\quad N(\text{RB})=3\cdot2=6,\quad N(\text{BB})=\binom{2}{2}=1.\]

  2. The counts add to \(10=\binom{5}{2}\). Conditioning on equal colours keeps four of those physical pairs:

    \[P(\text{RR}\mid\text{same colour})=\frac{3}{3+1}=\frac{3}{4}.\]

    The two visible same-colour types are not equally likely.

blocks.html: Forgetting a detail preserves uniformity only with constant multiplicity. If every visible outcome has the same number of equally likely physical versions, their probabilities are equal. If the numbers differ, keep the physical versions or attach the correct weights to the visible outcomes.

The same issue appears when forming committees. Choosing a senior chair uniformly, then choosing the remaining members uniformly, makes the chair-recorded routes equally likely. After the chair is forgotten, a committee with more eligible senior chairs is more likely to appear. Choosing uniformly among all admissible committees would be a different experiment.

For the earlier five-senior, three-junior example, uniformly choosing an admissible committee gives probability \(\frac{30}{55}=\frac{6}{11}\) of exactly two seniors. Uniformly choosing a senior chair and two other members gives \(\frac{2(30)}{105}=\frac{4}{7}\) instead. State which random choice the question specifies.

Do not mix an ordered numerator with an unordered denominator. Converting both may leave a probability unchanged if the same constant factor applies. Converting only one changes the probability, and a factor that varies between outcomes cannot simply be cancelled.

sections.title: Which integer values satisfy the original counting model?
sections.label: Inverse counts
sections.intro:
When the number of available objects is unknown, first translate the wording into a count or a ratio of counts. Record the minimum capacity and integer domain before cancelling factorials. A probability equation additionally requires a positive total or conditioning count.

Factorial ratios can make the algebra short:

\[\frac{\binom{n}{r+1}}{\binom{n}{r}}=\frac{n-r}{r+1},\qquad n,r\in\mathbb{Z},\quad0\le r<n.\]

The denominator is then nonzero. Other inverse questions may produce several algebraic roots; preserve them until their integer, capacity and original-model conditions are checked.

blocks.title: Check the integer parameter in both original counts
blocks.prompt: For \(n\ge4\) distinct people, the number of four-person committees is three times the number of three-person committees. Find \(n\), then give the four-person committee count as a check.
blocks.hint: Use \(\frac{\binom{n}{4}}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{n-3}{4}\), or expand the factorials. The stated domain justifies cancelling the nonzero three-person count.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\binom{n}{4}=3\binom{n}{3},\qquad\frac{n-3}{4}=3,\qquad n=15.\]
  2. \[\binom{15}{4}=1365,\qquad3\binom{15}{3}=3(455)=1365.\]

    The integer value satisfies the capacity requirement and the original equation.

blocks.html: Finish with the original statement. Give the admissible integer value, substitute it into the original count or probability, and show that both sides agree. A decimal approximation to a noninteger root is not a possible number of people.

A reliable final ledger records the outcome, the construction choices, every case restriction, the overcount multiplicity if one exists, and the probability denominator when needed. This single habit connects arrangements, selections, role assignments and conditional counting without relying on isolated formula keywords.

glossary.definition: The complete information the question records after all choices have been made.
One sequence of choices used to produce a final outcome.
The number of construction routes or labelled versions representing one final outcome.
A selected person satisfying the conditions for a particular role.
A named job whose holder remains part of the final outcome.
The numbers of selected objects or people belonging to each category.
Cases that cannot contain the same final outcome.
The outcomes satisfying two restrictions at the same time.
An outcome retaining the identities of the actual selected objects.
An outcome recording only the displayed symbols or categories, possibly combining several physical outcomes.
A random choice giving every outcome in the stated sample space the same probability.
A value satisfying the integer, capacity and probability conditions of the original problem.

examples.title: A temporary leader counts every committee three times
examples.question: Choose a three-person committee from eight distinct people. One proposed method first chooses a temporary leader, then two other members. The final committee has no leader. How many committees are there, and why must the proposed count be divided?
solution:
Choosing a temporary leader and then two members gives

\[8\binom{7}{2}=168.\]

This counts a committee together with a marked member. It does not yet count unmarked committees.
Take one committee, for example \(\{A,B,C\}\). The construction can mark A, B or C. Every three-person committee has exactly three such marked versions.

\[N=\frac{8\binom{7}{2}}{3}=56=\binom{8}{3}.\]

The divisor is the number of temporary leader choices inside each finished committee. If an actual leader were required as part of the final outcome, the answer would remain \(168\).

examples.title: Eligible leaders create unequal construction multiplicities
examples.question: Five seniors and three juniors are available. Choose a three-person committee containing at least one senior. Compare the number of committees with the number of outcomes in which a senior chair is also recorded.
solution:
Split by the number \(j\) of seniors. The cases \(j=1,2,3\) are disjoint and cover every permitted committee:

\[N_1=\binom{5}{1}\binom{3}{2}=15,\quad N_2=\binom{5}{2}\binom{3}{1}=30,\quad N_3=\binom{5}{3}\binom{3}{0}=10.\]

\[N_{\text{committees}}=15+30+10=55.\]

As a check, remove the sole all-junior committee from all \(\binom{8}{3}=56\) committees.

A committee with \(j\) seniors has \(j\) possible senior chairs. Recording the chair gives

\[N_{\text{chair recorded}}=1(15)+2(30)+3(10)=105.\]

Choosing the senior chair first also gives \(5\binom{7}{2}=105\). Forgetting that chair does not have one common multiplicity: different committees occur once, twice or three times. Dividing \(105\) by three would therefore not recover the \(55\) committees.

examples.title: The number of eligible role assignments depends on composition
examples.question: Four seniors and three juniors form a four-person team. The team must contain at least two seniors. A captain and a different deputy are chosen from its senior members, and the two roles are recorded. Count the outcomes.
solution:
Let \(j\) be the number of seniors in the team. Its possible values are \(2,3,4\). Choose its members, then fill the two different roles:

\[N_j=\binom{4}{j}\binom{3}{4-j}\,j(j-1).\]

The factor \(j(j-1)\) chooses the captain and then a different deputy from the selected seniors.

\[N=36+72+12=120.\]

The role choices vary with the senior composition, so they belong inside the case count.

A second complete construction chooses the ordered senior captain and deputy first, in \(4\cdot3\) ways, and then chooses any two of the five remaining people:

\[4\cdot3\binom{5}{2}=120.\]

Every resulting team contains the two required seniors and has one recorded captain and deputy; it is counted exactly once.

examples.title: Exactly one restriction requires removing the overlap twice
examples.question: Seven distinct people A, B, C, D, E, F and G sit in a straight line. Count arrangements in which at least one of the pairs AB and CD is adjacent, and arrangements in which exactly one of those pairs is adjacent. Each pair may appear in either order.
solution:
Let \(E\) mean that A and B are adjacent and \(F\) mean that C and D are adjacent. Treating one pair as a block gives

\[N(E)=2\cdot6!=1440,\qquad N(F)=1440.\]

For both events, use two blocks and the three remaining people. Each block has two internal orders:

\[N(E\cap F)=2^2\cdot5!=480.\]

At least one means the union. The sum of the individual counts includes the overlap twice, so subtract it once:

\[N(E\cup F)=1440+1440-480=2400.\]

Exactly one excludes the overlap completely. Count E only and F only:

\[N(\text{exactly one})=(1440-480)+(1440-480)=1920.\]

Equivalently subtract twice the overlap from \(N(E)+N(F)\). This statement says nothing about whether other people happen to sit adjacent.

examples.title: Split a digit construction where the leading-zero rule changes
examples.question: How many four-digit numbers can be made from \(0,1,2,3,4,5\), without repeating any digit, if the number is divisible by five and contains at least one of the digits two and four?
solution: A multiple of five ends in zero or five. These are disjoint final-digit cases. Count each case separately because zero remains available for the first position only in the second case.

Last digit zero. Fill the first three positions from the five nonzero digits: \(5\cdot4\cdot3=60\). Numbers containing neither two nor four must use the three digits one, three and five in those positions, giving \(3!=6\).

\[N_0=60-6=54.\]

Last digit five. The first digit has four choices, one to four. Then the two middle positions have four and three choices:

\[N_{5,\text{all}}=4\cdot4\cdot3=48.\]

If neither two nor four appears, the first three positions use zero, one and three. There are \(3!-2!=4\) valid orders after removing the two with leading zero.

\[N_5=48-4=44.\]

\[N=N_0+N_5=54+44=98.\]

The condition “at least one” includes numbers containing both two and four. Subtracting the complementary case avoids counting those twice.

examples.title: Visible outcomes need not be equally likely
examples.question: A bag contains four physical tiles labelled \(A_1,A_2,B,C\); the first two both display the letter A. Two tiles are selected uniformly from all unordered physical pairs. Find the probability that both display A, given that at least one displays A.
solution:
There are \(\binom{4}{2}=6\) equally likely physical pairs. Grouping them by their visible letters gives:

Visible lettersPhysical pair count
AA\(1\)
AB\(2\)
AC\(2\)
BC\(1\)

The condition excludes only the pair \(\{B,C\}\). Five physical pairs remain equally likely; one is \(\{A_1,A_2\}\).

\[P(\text{AA}\mid\text{at least one A})=\frac{1}{5}.\]
Counting only the three permitted visible types AA, AB and AC and using \(\frac{1}{3}\) would change the random experiment. AB and AC each have two physical representations, while AA has one.

If a different experiment explicitly chose uniformly from the visible types AA, AB, AC and BC, then conditioning on an A would give \(\frac{1}{3}\). The wording defining the random choice decides which probability model applies.

examples.title: Recover an integer parameter and replay the original count
examples.question: From \(n\) distinct people, the number of three-person committees is twice the number of two-person committees. Find \(n\), assuming \(n\ge3\).
solution:
Translate the given comparison into counts:

\[\binom{n}{3}=2\binom{n}{2},\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z},\quad n\ge3.\]

\[\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}=2\cdot \frac{n(n-1)}{2}.\]

Because \(n\ge3\), the common factor \(n(n-1)\) is nonzero and can be cancelled.

Check the original model:

\[\binom{8}{3}=56,\qquad2\binom{8}{2}=2(28)=56.\]

The value is an admissible integer and satisfies the original comparison. If the multiplied polynomial is solved without respecting the stated domain, the roots zero and one can also appear; they do not describe this problem.

extraPractice.title: Roles change the weighting of committees
extraPractice.prompt: A panel of four is selected from three distinct seniors and five distinct juniors. At least one senior must be selected. The panel has a senior chair and a secretary who is any other panel member. Count the possible panels when roles are ignored, and then the complete outcomes recording both the panel and its two role holders. A complete outcome is selected uniformly from the latter set. Find the probability that its panel contains exactly two seniors.
extraPractice.hint: A panel containing \(k\) seniors has \(3k\) possible chair-secretary assignments. This multiplicity is not constant across all panels. Alternatively, choose the senior chair, choose the secretary, then choose the two remaining members.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N_{\text{panels}}=\binom{8}{4}-\binom{5}{4}=70-5=65.\]

  2. Choose a senior chair in three ways, a secretary from the remaining seven people, and the other two members from the remaining six:

    \[N_{\text{roles}}=3\cdot7\binom{6}{2}=315.\]

    Each complete outcome has exactly one chair, one secretary and one residual pair, so this construction counts it once.

  3. For exactly two seniors, first select the panel, then assign its roles:

    \[N_2=\binom{3}{2}\binom{5}{2}\cdot2\cdot3=180.\]
  4. \[P(\text{exactly two seniors})=\frac{180}{315}=\frac{4}{7}.\]

    Uniformly selecting a panel first and then assigning its roles would define a different experiment. Here the complete role-bearing outcomes are explicitly equally likely.

extraPractice.title: Use the last digit and the zero position as separate cases
extraPractice.prompt: A four-digit number is formed using four different digits from \(0,1,2,3,4,5,6\). The first digit cannot be zero. Count the even numbers, the even numbers containing zero, and all allowed numbers containing zero. A number is selected uniformly from all allowed four-digit numbers. Find the probability that it is even given that it contains zero.
extraPractice.hint: Separate numbers ending in zero from those ending in \(2,4\) or \(6\). If a nonzero even digit is last and zero occurs, zero must occupy one of the two middle positions.
extraPractice.solution:
1. If the last digit is zero, the other positions have \(6,5,4\) choices. If the last digit is one of the three nonzero even digits, the first position has five choices and the middle positions have five then four:

    \[N(E)=6\cdot5\cdot4+3\cdot5\cdot5\cdot4=120+300=420.\]

  2. For an even number containing zero, the zero-ending case still contributes \(120\). In the other case choose the nonzero last digit, the middle position of zero, the first digit and the remaining middle digit:

    \[N(E\cap Z)=120+3\cdot2\cdot5\cdot4=240.\]

  3. For all allowed numbers containing zero, choose one of the three non-leading positions for zero, then fill the remaining positions with distinct nonzero digits:

    \[N(Z)=3\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4=360.\]
  4. \[P(E\mid Z)=\frac{240}{360}=\frac{2}{3}.\]

    The conditioning event allows odd as well as even final digits. Its count is not the even-number total.

extraPractice.title: Two repeated pairs produce an overlap
extraPractice.prompt: All six letters of AABBCD are arranged in a line. An outcome is a visible string, so the two As are indistinguishable and the two Bs are indistinguishable. Count the strings in which the As are adjacent and those in which both the As and the Bs are adjacent. A distinct visible string is selected uniformly. Find the probability that the Bs are adjacent given that the As are not adjacent.

fields.label: Bs adjacent given As not adjacent

extraPractice.hint: Use an AA block for the first count and AA and BB blocks for their overlap. The conditional numerator excludes the overlap from the B-adjacent count.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N(\Omega)=\frac{6!}{2!2!}=180.\]

    The denominator removes the two identical A labels and the two identical B labels.

  2. For adjacent As, the objects are AA, B, B, C and D:

    \[N(A)=\frac{5!}{2!}=60.\]

    The same reasoning gives \(N(B)=60\).

  3. For both pairs adjacent, AA, BB, C and D are four distinct objects:

    \[N(A\cap B)=4!=24.\]
  4. \[P(B\mid A^{\mathrm c})=\frac{N(B)-N(A\cap B)}{N(\Omega)-N(A)}=\frac{60-24}{180-60}=\frac{3}{10}.\]

    Subtract the overlap from the numerator as well as removing the forbidden A-adjacent strings from the denominator.

extraPractice.title: A named exclusion is applied inside the category condition
extraPractice.prompt: A committee of four is chosen from four distinct arts students and five distinct science students. It must contain at least one student from each category. A is one specified arts student and B is one specified science student. Count all committees satisfying the category rule and those also satisfying the rule that A and B are not both selected. A committee is selected uniformly from the committees satisfying both rules. Find the probability that A is selected.
extraPractice.hint: Remove all-arts and all-science committees. A committee containing both A and B already satisfies the category rule. If A is selected but B is excluded, retain at least one of the remaining science students.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N(M)=\binom{9}{4}-\binom{4}{4}-\binom{5}{4}=126-1-5=120.\]

    The two excluded cases are disjoint.

  2. Fix A and B. The other two members can be any pair from the remaining seven:

    \[N(M\text{ and not both A,B})=120-\binom{7}{2}=99.\]

  3. To include A and exclude B, choose the other three members from three arts and four science students. Remove the one choice containing only arts students:

    \[N(\text{A selected and both rules})=\binom{7}{3}-\binom{3}{3}=34.\]
  4. \[P(\text{A selected}\mid\text{both rules})=\frac{34}{99}.\]

    The restriction does not mean that A and B must both be absent; either one may be selected.

extraPractice.title: State the integer domain before cancelling
extraPractice.prompt: There are \(n\) distinct students, where \(n\ge3\) is an integer. The number of ways to assign three different students to the distinct roles of chair, secretary and treasurer is four times the number of ways to choose an unordered pair of students. Find \(n\), the number of unordered pairs, and the number of three-role assignments.
extraPractice.hint: Write the ordered role count as \(n(n-1)(n-2)\), and the unordered pair count as \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). The stated domain makes the cancelled factor nonzero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[n(n-1)(n-2)=4\binom{n}{2}=2n(n-1),\qquad n\in\mathbb Z,\quad n\ge3.\]

  2. Since \(n(n-1)>0\), cancel that factor:

    \[n-2=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=4.\]
  3. \[\binom{4}{2}=6,\qquad {}^4P_3=4\cdot3\cdot2=24=4\cdot6.\]

    The check verifies the original counting relation. The algebraic values zero and one from a factored polynomial would not satisfy the original domain.

extraPractice.title: Selection changes the order count
extraPractice.prompt: Choose and order two of five speakers. If A is chosen, A must speak first. How many programmes are possible?
extraPractice.hint: Four programmes start with A. Without A, there are four choices for the first speaker and three for the second.
extraPractice.solution:
Four programmes start with A. Without A, there are four choices for the first speaker and three for the second.

  • Answer: \(16\)

extraPractice.title: Count physical outcomes
extraPractice.prompt: Choose two counters from three red and two blue counters, with all physical pairs equally likely. Find the probability both are red.
extraPractice.hint: The numerator counts pairs from the three red counters. The denominator counts all pairs of the five counters.
extraPractice.solution:
The numerator counts pairs from the three red counters. The denominator counts all pairs of the five counters.

  • Answer: \(\frac{3}{10}\)

extraPractice.title: Correct the overlap
extraPractice.prompt: Four different pupils stand in line. Count the arrangements in which X is adjacent to Y or to Z, including both.
extraPractice.hint: Each adjacency event has twice three factorial orders. In the overlap X is in the middle of a block with Y and Z. There are four overlap orders.
extraPractice.solution:
Each adjacency event has twice three factorial orders. In the overlap X is in the middle of a block with Y and Z. There are four overlap orders.

  • Answer: \(20\)

extraPractice.title: Use the conditional sample space
extraPractice.prompt: Choose two from two boys and three girls. Given at least one girl was chosen, find the probability both selected pupils are girls.
extraPractice.hint: Exclude the all-boy pair from the denominator. The numerator is the number of two-girl pairs.
extraPractice.solution:
Exclude the all-boy pair from the denominator. The numerator is the number of two-girl pairs.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{3}\)

starters.title: Team composition controls the two eligible roles
starters.question: A team of five is selected from four distinct musicians and five distinct athletes. Every person belongs to exactly one category. The team has a musician captain and an athlete deputy. A complete outcome records the selected members, captain and deputy; all complete outcomes are equally likely. Count all complete outcomes and those with at least three athletes. M is one specified musician and A is one specified athlete. Count the complete outcomes in which M and A are not both selected. Given this last condition, find the probability that the team contains exactly two musicians.
starters.hint: A team with \(k\) musicians has \(k(5-k)\) captain-deputy assignments. Use composition cases when imposing membership conditions. For the unrestricted total, choose the two role holders first.
starters.solution:
1. Choose the musician captain, athlete deputy and three other members:

    \[N(\Omega)=4\cdot5\binom{7}{3}=700.\]

  2. At least three athletes means one or two musicians, since the captain must be a musician. The disjoint counts are

    \[N_1=\binom{4}{1}\binom{5}{4}\cdot1\cdot4=80,\]\[N_2=\binom{4}{2}\binom{5}{3}\cdot2\cdot3=360.\]

    The requested count is \(80+360=440\).

  3. For M and A both selected, let \(k\) be the musician count. Select the other members and then the roles:

    \[N(M,A\text{ both})=\sum_{k=1}^{4}\binom{3}{k-1}\binom{4}{4-k}k(5-k).\]

    The four terms are \(16,108,72,4\), giving \(200\) complete outcomes. Therefore

    \[N(F)=700-200=500.\]

  4. Of the \(360\) outcomes with two musicians, the \(k=2\) term counts \(108\) containing both specified people. Thus

    \[N(\text{two musicians}\cap F)=360-108=252.\]
  5. \[P(\text{two musicians}\mid F)=\frac{252}{500}=\frac{63}{125}.\]

    Different team compositions permit different numbers of role assignments. Counting unweighted teams would describe a different random experiment.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: choose the two eligible role holders first for the unrestricted count.
  • 1 mark: obtain 700 complete outcomes.
  • 1 mark: split the at-least-three-athletes event into one- and two-musician cases.
  • 1 mark: include the role multiplicities and obtain 440.
  • 1 mark: express the both-specified-members count by team composition.
  • 1 mark: obtain the four contributions 16, 108, 72 and 4.
  • 1 mark: subtract their sum to obtain the conditioning count 500.
  • 1 mark: exclude 108 from the two-musician count to obtain 252.
  • 1 mark: divide counts referring to the same complete-outcome sample space.
  • 1 mark: obtain the simplified conditional probability.

starters.title: A zero, an even ending and a moving odd block
starters.question: A code consists of six different digits chosen from \(0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\). Its first digit is nonzero and it contains exactly two odd digits. Count all such codes and those whose last digit is even. Among codes whose last digit is even, count those in which the two odd digits are adjacent. A code is selected uniformly from all codes satisfying the original rules. Find the probability that its odd digits are adjacent given that its last digit is even.
starters.hint: Exactly two odd digits forces all four even digits, including zero, to be used. Choose the odd pair first. For the ending restriction, separate a zero ending from a nonzero even ending. An odd-digit block has two internal orders.
starters.solution:
1. Choose the odd pair in \(\binom{4}{2}=6\) ways. For each pair, all six chosen digits are distinct, with zero present. Exclude arrangements beginning with zero:

    \[N(\Omega)=\binom{4}{2}(6!-5!)=6(600)=3600.\]

  2. Fix a chosen odd pair. If the last digit is zero, the remaining five nonzero digits have \(5!=120\) orders. If the last digit is a nonzero even digit, choose it in three ways; the first digit then has four nonzero choices and the remaining four positions have \(4!\) orders:

    \[N(E)=6\bigl(120+3\cdot4\cdot4!\bigr)=6(408)=2448.\]

  3. Now join the two odd digits into one block, retaining their two internal orders. For each chosen odd pair and a zero ending, the remaining four units have \(4!\) orders, contributing \(2\cdot4!=48\).

  4. For each of the three nonzero even endings, the four remaining units include zero and the odd block. Their permissible orders are \(4!-3!\), since zero cannot be first. With two internal block orders this contributes \(3\cdot2(4!-3!)=108\).

    \[N(J\cap E)=6(48+108)=936.\]
  5. \[P(J\mid E)=\frac{936}{2448}=\frac{13}{34}.\]

    The block can occupy different positions but cannot end the code, because the ending is even. The two ending cases cover every valid construction once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: infer that all four even digits must be included and choose the odd pair.
  • 1 mark: remove leading-zero arrangements and obtain 3600.
  • 1 mark: split even endings into zero and nonzero cases.
  • 1 mark: obtain the correct contributions and total 2448.
  • 1 mark: introduce the odd block with its two internal orders.
  • 1 mark: obtain the zero-ending block contribution 48 per odd pair.
  • 1 mark: exclude a leading zero in the nonzero-ending block case.
  • 1 mark: combine the cases and odd-pair choices to obtain 936.
  • 1 mark: use the even-ending denominator and simplify the conditional probability.

revision.body:
Describe one finished outcome, then make every construction count it the right number of times.

Does my construction remember something the outcome forgets?

Count selections, role assignments and position orders separately. Divide a route count only when every finished outcome has the same positive number \(m\) of valid routes:

\[N_{\text{outcomes}}=\frac{N_{\text{routes}}}{m}.\]

A forgotten leader gives \(r\) routes per \(r\)-person group only when every member could have been that leader. A qualification restriction can make the multiplicity vary.

Do role choices depend on composition?

A team of size \(r\) with \(k\) eligible chairs has \(k\) chair choices. If its deputy must come from the other category, there are \(k(r-k)\) role assignments. Sum the weighted counts over valid compositions. Roles remain named even when their holders come from the same category.

\[N=\sum_k N(\text{composition }k)\,N(\text{roles}\mid k).\]

Are my cases disjoint and exhaustive?

\[N(A\cup B)=N(A)+N(B)-N(A\cap B).\]

Separate special final digits, zero positions or category counts before multiplying. Leading zeroes are forbidden for ordinary numbers. Blocks need their internal orders; repeated visible symbols do not. “Not both” allows either one and differs from “neither”.

What is uniform, and what is given?

\[P(E\mid F)=\frac{N(E\cap F)}{N(F)},\qquad N(F)>0.\]

Both counts must use the same equally likely elementary outcomes. Physical labelled objects can give visible patterns unequal weights. A uniform team and a uniform team-with-roles need not be the same experiment. For inverse counts, state the integer domain, solve, then check the original relation.
revision.checks: • Finished outcome; constant multiplicity; eligible roles; disjoint cases; repeated identities; uniform space; given event; integer domain.
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.
